sections.intent: The 5Ps formulation of the vignette, with each factor meeting the intervention that targets it: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective and presenting. sources.harvard: Ajnakina, O., Stubbs, B., Francis, E., Gaughran, F., David, A. S., Murray, R. M. & Lally, J. (2021) Employment and relationship outcomes in first-episode psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies. *Schizophrenia Research*, 231: 122-133. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2021.03.013 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 15,272 people with a diagnosis of first-episode psychosis (range 20-1,724 per study) followed in 74 longitudinal studies, mean follow-up 8.3 years (SD 7.2); high- and middle-income countries, European and non-European
sources.perspective: psychiatric epidemiology and social outcomes research / random-effects meta-analysis of longitudinal cohorts with meta-regression
sources.use: Puts functional loss in the perpetuating box with a trajectory rather than a snapshot, since employment falls as follow-up lengthens, but it measures employment and relationships only and never the vignette's education.
sources.title: Employment and relationship outcomes in first-episode psychosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis restricted to LONGITUDINAL studies, pooling 74 cohorts and 15,272 first-episode cases over a mean 8.3 years of follow-up, with meta-regression of moderators. It can establish the scale of functional loss after a first episode in the only design that can: roughly a third are employed and a fifth in a relationship at the end of follow-up, and the employed proportion falls as follow-up lengthens. It also establishes that the pattern is culturally conditional, with higher employment but lower partnership rates in high-income and European settings than in middle-income and non-European ones. It cannot attribute the loss to the illness: these are proportions in exposed cohorts without matched general-population comparators in the pooled analysis, so it quantifies outcome, not causal effect, and it says nothing about education, which it does not measure. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so heterogeneity, risk of bias and publication-bias tests are unverified, and because pooling 74 cohorts with follow-ups ranging from short to decades-long is heterogeneous by construction.

sources.harvard: Andreasen, N. C., Carpenter, W. T., Kane, J. M., Lasser, R. A., Marder, S. R. & Weinberger, D. R. (2005) Remission in schizophrenia: proposed criteria and rationale for consensus. *The American Journal of Psychiatry*, 162 (3): 441-449. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.3.441 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no recruited participants - an expert working group's review of existing definitions and assessment instruments
sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry / expert consensus statement on outcome definition
sources.use: Gives e1-what the field's definition of remission as a symptom level maintained over time rather than an amount of change, and warns e1-assess and e1-limits that papers citing these criteria often drop the duration requirement.
sources.title: Remission in schizophrenia: proposed criteria and rationale for consensus
sources.strength_why: The paper that established the first consensus-based operational criteria for symptomatic remission in schizophrenia, and the one almost every later cohort cites when it says a participant was 'in remission' - including `notes/okeeffe-2021-meaning-in-life-fep.md`, which applies these criteria at 20-year follow-up. It can establish what the field agreed remission means and why it chose thresholds maintained over time rather than change scores. It cannot establish that the criteria are valid, that they predict anything, or that they capture recovery as opposed to symptom level: the authors themselves call the approach novel and say it 'will require further examination of its validity and utility, as well as future refinement, particularly in relation to psychosocial and cognitive function and dysfunction'. Indicative, which is the right tier for an expert consensus statement used for a concept: it is authoritative about a definition and it is not evidence. Rated from the abstract alone - the full text is paywalled - so the specific item thresholds and the six-month duration requirement are recorded here only where a second source in the corpus states them.

sources.harvard: Arnold, C., Villagonzalo, K.-A., Meyer, D., Farhall, J., Foley, F., Kyrios, M. & Thomas, N. (2019) Predicting engagement with an online psychosocial intervention for psychosis: exploring individual- and intervention-level predictors. *Internet Interventions*, 18: 100266. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.invent.2019.100266 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: adults 18-65 with a SCID-confirmed nonorganic psychotic disorder in the past 2 years, recruited through community mental health services and Facebook, Victoria, Australia
sources.perspective: clinical psychology and digital mental health / secondary analysis of randomised conditions with website log data
sources.dataset: Self-Management and Recovery Technology (SMART) research programme, Australia
sources.use: Settles a design detail rather than a decision: a self-guided site alone gets limited engagement and light human contact roughly quadrupled it, so a digital component is defensible as digital plus a person, not instead of one.
sources.title: Predicting engagement with an online psychosocial intervention for psychosis: Exploring individual- and intervention-level predictors
sources.strength_why: A prospective study of 98 adults with SCID-confirmed psychosis in which the key predictor, asynchronous email support, was randomised and engagement was measured objectively from website logs rather than self-report, so it can establish that light-touch human support raises use of a self-guided online intervention in this population and that externally controlled motivation moderates that effect. It cannot establish that more use produces better clinical outcomes, because no outcome was measured here and the authors say the dose-response relationship may not be linear; nor can it generalise to routine care, because the sample was research-recruited, internet-confident and screened. Moderate rather than strong: the randomised comparison is sound but the sample is small, the predictor set was analysed observationally, and one table is internally inconsistent (see Limitations).

sources.harvard: Bailey, T., Alvarez-Jimenez, M., Garcia-Sanchez, A. M., Hulbert, C., Barlow, E. & Bendall, S. (2018) Childhood trauma is associated with severity of hallucinations and delusions in psychotic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 44 (5): 1111-1122. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbx161 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 4680 participants with a diagnosed psychotic disorder, pooled from 29 meta-analysed studies out of 41 meeting inclusion criteria
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / systematic review and meta-analysis of correlational studies
sources.use: Takes the adversity strand past risk of onset to symptom severity, and bounds it: the unexpected null for negative symptoms confines the trauma argument to hallucinations and delusions.
sources.title: Childhood trauma is associated with severity of hallucinations and delusions in psychotic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review screening 6667 studies to 41, meta-analysing 29 with 4680 participants, with reporting bias and quality assessed and unpublished data sought from authors. It moves the trauma argument one step past risk of onset — which Varese et al. (2012) already covers — to severity of specific symptoms: childhood trauma correlates with hallucination severity (r = .199) and delusion severity (r = .172), both P < .001. It also delivers a result the authors did NOT expect and report as such: trauma was not correlated with negative-symptom severity (r = .049, P = .095), while neglect specifically was (r = .142, P = .005). It CANNOT establish that trauma shapes the CONTENT of psychotic experience — severity is not content, and nothing here addresses what the voices or delusions are about. Nor can it establish direction: the pooled studies are correlational, and the effects are small (r around .17 to .20, roughly 3-4% of variance). Moderate on design, with a clear ceiling on what it may be asked to say.

sources.strength_why: Nationally representative US survey data from economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, Vanderbilt and Harvard — far better than a company press figure for establishing adoption. sources.harvard: Birdsey, N. & Kustner, C. (2021) Reviewing the Social GRACES: what do they add and limit in systemic thinking and practice? *The American Journal of Family Therapy*, 49 (5): 429-442. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1080/01926187.2020.1830731 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no participants; a review of the systemic-practice and family-therapy literature, with one illustrative clinical supervision case from UK practice
sources.perspective: systemic family therapy and clinical psychology / critical narrative review
sources.use: The citable peer-reviewed route to Burnham's GRACES, and useful mainly for the critical move it licenses, since its own objection that the list is reductive and linear applies equally to the 5Ps.
sources.title: Reviewing the Social GRACES: What do they add and limit in systemic thinking and practice?
sources.strength_why: A peer-reviewed review that traces the Social GRACES to named origins — Burnham (1992, 1993) and Roper-Hall (1998), via the earlier 'DISGRRACCE' mnemonic — lists the current fifteen graces, and then sets out four substantive criticisms: that the framework is restrictively linear, that it is reductive and risks becoming 'a list of areas of difference', that therapists privilege the graces inside their own comfort zone, and that the current fifteen omit disablism. It can establish what the GRACES are, where they came from and what they are criticised for, which is exactly what a cultural-considerations paragraph needs. It CANNOT establish that using them changes clinical outcomes: there is no trial, no outcome measure and no psychosis population anywhere in it, and the single clinical illustration is one anonymised supervision case written up by the authors. Indicative on design.

It can establish that the intervention is deliverable and acceptable, which it does convincingly, but its clinical effect sizes carry almost no evidential weight and the authors say so repeatedly.

sources.population: not applicable — review of 43 sources spanning 1810 to 2026
sources.perspective: psychiatry / narrative review with historical synthesis
sources.use: Changes the thesis rather than supporting it, supplying the pathoplastic/pathogenic distinction and the open question about form, and it is the route to Burns, Flathers and Hudon whose figures the corpus holds at second hand.
sources.title: Technology-Themed Persecutory and Related Presentations of Delusions in the Digital Age: Narrative Review
sources.strength_why: The best-conducted review in the corpus: three databases with no date restriction, SANRA-informed synthesis, an explicit typology, a chronological evidence table, and a limitations section that names the circularity in its own central hypothesis. Still a narrative review with no risk-of-bias assessment and a self-selecting case literature, and the authors say both.

(2025) 'The algorithm is hacked': analysis of technology delusions in a modern-day cohort. *The British Journal of Psychiatry*, advance online publication: 1-5. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.2025.10452 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry / retrospective chart review with logistic regression
sources.dataset: UCLA Thought Disorders Intensive Outpatient Program records 2016-2024
sources.use: The primary for the 51.7 per cent figure the corpus currently carries through Bokhari, and the trend anchor for pathoplasticity; nobody was followed and no exposure measured, so it is worthless as aetiology.
sources.title: 'The algorithm is hacked': analysis of technology delusions in a modern-day cohort
sources.strength_why: A single-centre retrospective chart review of 228 adults with psychosis that supplies the only year-on-year trend estimate in the corpus for technology-themed delusional content, and rich verbatim description of its subtypes. It can establish that technology themes are common in a contemporary psychosis service and that they became more likely across 2016-2024 in this sample; it cannot establish population prevalence, cause, or that technology contributed to the delusions, because the sample is a selected, housed, insured, substance-abstinent day-programme cohort and the data were never collected for research. The tier is held at moderate rather than higher by the design, by the authors' own point that rising clinician awareness could itself produce the trend, and by an unexplained discrepancy between the group sizes in Table 1 and the counts in the Results text (see Limitations).

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / retrospective archival records study
sources.dataset: archival records of one US state psychiatric facility, 20th century
sources.use: Pairs with Skodlar to give pathoplasticity two independent national archives, but the technology figures the corpus quotes from it are absent from the abstract, which makes it the one most worth paying to read.
sources.title: Delusion content across the 20th century in an American psychiatric hospital
sources.strength_why: A retrospective archival study of 102 records, sampled by decade from a single US state psychiatric hospital, which can show that delusional content in an American sample tracked sociocultural change in the same way non-American samples had. It cannot support any statement about frequency in a population, nor about technology specifically, because the sample is tiny per decade, confined to one institution, and the abstract reports no technology-specific result at all. Indicative rather than moderate because of the per-decade cell sizes and because the appraisal rests on the abstract alone.

sources.harvard: Cantor-Graae, E. & Selten, J. P. (2005) Schizophrenia and migration: a meta-analysis and review. *American Journal of Psychiatry*, 162 (1): 12-24. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.1.12 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: population-based incidence studies of migrant groups, published 1977-2003; 40 effect sizes for first-generation migrants, 7 for second-generation, 50 in the combined analysis
sources.perspective: social psychiatry / meta-analysis of population-based incidence studies
sources.use: Anchors the migration strand because the subgroup pattern — higher risk in the second generation than the first — is what no genetic or selective-migration explanation handles, though its figures are foundational rather than current.
sources.title: Schizophrenia and migration: a meta-analysis and review.
sources.strength_why: A mixed-effects meta-analysis of population-based incidence studies that established the size of the migrant excess in schizophrenia — relative risk 2.7 (95% CI 2.3-3.2) for first-generation and 4.5 (95% CI 1.5-13.1) for second-generation migrants — and found it graded by the migrant group's region of origin and skin colour, which is the finding that pushed the field towards psychosocial rather than genetic explanations. It cannot establish causation and the second-generation estimate rests on only 7 effect sizes with an interval from 1.5 to 13.1. Moderate rather than strong because the search was MEDLINE-only, English-language-only, and now over twenty years out of date; its figures are superseded by later reviews and it should be cited as the foundational finding rather than the current estimate.

sources.use: Makes antipsychotic discontinuation the most parsimonious explanation for the Basaran case at 24 against 61 per cent relapse, and is the pole against which Wunderink is read, because it tests stopping and not supervised tapering.
sources.title: Maintenance treatment with antipsychotic drugs for schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 75 placebo-controlled RCTs and 9145 participants with GRADE certainty ratings, reporting the relapse-prevention effect as high-certainty evidence: 24% relapse on drug versus 61% on placebo at seven to twelve months (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.45, NNTB 3), with hospitalisation reduced from 18% to 7% (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.57, NNTB 8). It also quantifies the harms in the same currency — movement disorders 14% versus 8% (RR 1.52, NNTH 20), sedation and weight gain — which is what makes it usable for a shared decision rather than an argument for medication. It CANNOT answer the vignette's actual question: the population is schizophrenia broadly rather than first episode, the evidence runs 'approximately up to two years of follow-up' and no further, the suicide and employment analyses are underpowered and low-certainty, and randomisation, allocation and blinding were 'poorly reported' in many included studies. Strong on design and on the authors' own GRADE rating of the primary outcome.

sources.title: Impact of case formulation in cognitive behaviour therapy for psychosis.
sources.strength_why: The only empirical test of case formulation in psychosis I could locate, and it is a largely NULL and partly adverse result: across two experiments, formulation 'had little or no impact' on perceived therapeutic relationship, on strength of delusional and self-evaluative beliefs, or on anxiety and depression; therapists' own ratings of the relationship improved while clients' did not, and six clients found formulation at least in part a negative experience. It can therefore establish that a formulation-led plan should not be presented as an intervention with demonstrated benefit, which is a real constraint on `e2-plan`. It CANNOT establish that formulation is useless — it is small, uncontrolled, single-site, from one service, over twenty years old and predates the Five Ps version of the framework, and the abstract does not report the sample size. Indicative on design; its FIT to the claim that a formulation-based plan is justified is high precisely because it qualifies it.

sources.title: Relapse prediction in schizophrenia with smartphone digital phenotyping during COVID-19: a prospective, three-site, two-country, longitudinal study.
sources.strength_why: A prospective, three-site, two-country smartphone cohort (132 participants, 76 with schizophrenia and 56 controls, mean 156 days of enrolment) in which 20 clinical relapses occurred and were ascertained from interviews and medical records. It can establish that passive smartphone data behave differently around relapse in a real outpatient population in both the United States and India - anomalies 2.12 times more frequent in the month before relapse and 2.78 times more frequent in the month around it, and 1.41 times more effective than a survey-only logistic regression - and it can establish, with the authors' own permutation test, that the method did not differ significantly between the Boston, Bangalore and Bhopal sites. It cannot establish that this is usable as a clinical alert: of 188 statistically significant anomalies, only 13 (6.9%) were true positives, so roughly 93% of flags were false, and the model was fitted retrospectively to prospectively collected data rather than deployed and tested. Rated moderate: the design is as close to a service test as this literature gets, 20 relapse events is a small outcome count, and the COVID-19 data collection window is a limitation the authors state at length.

sources.title: Comparison of early intervention services vs treatment as usual for early-phase psychosis: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-reported systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs and 2176 patients, with prespecified subgroup and meta-regression analyses and unpublished data obtained from the authors of every included trial, reporting risk ratios and standardised mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. It is the best available evidence that a coordinated multimodal service — not any single modality — outperforms ordinary care in early-phase psychosis, and its inclusion criteria define that service as combining psychosocial AND psychopharmacological components delivered by one team, which is the direct evidence that a plan touching several domains beats a referral chain. It CANNOT establish which component does the work: the unit of randomisation is the service, so the meta-analysis is silent on the contribution of medication, family work, vocational support or psychotherapy taken separately. It also cannot speak beyond 24 months, the longest trial duration included, and the protocol was 'predetermined but unpublished' rather than registered, which is a transparency weakness in an otherwise well-conducted review.

sources.title: Addicted, attached, or just delegating? A scoping review on 'problematic artificial intelligence use'
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-ScR scoping review with a registered protocol that maps the whole construct of problematic AI use across 37 empirical studies, and the only source found that answers the measurement question directly. It CAN establish that the construct exists in the literature but is not settled: terminology is inconsistent, definitions are frequently absent altogether in eight of the included studies, AI-specific instruments do exist — the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale, built on the DSM-5-TR Internet Gaming Disorder framework, and the AI Chatbot Dependence Scale — but most measurement borrows scales for social media, smartphones, mobile applications, computers and in one case fast food, which the authors argue 'presuppose rather than test' that problematic AI use has the same structure. It can also establish that the evidence base is 30 quantitative and 7 mixed-method studies, overwhelmingly cross-sectional. It CANNOT establish prevalence, direction or any causal claim, and the authors say so: 'The predominance of cross-sectional studies limits conclusions about the directionality of key associations ... precludes conclusions about whether, for instance, loneliness leads to problematic AI use or whether problematic AI use exacerbates loneliness.' Moderate rather than strong: a transparent, registered scoping review with a careful construct critique, but a scoping review performs no risk-of-bias assessment by design, searched only Web of Science and Scopus, and was restricted to English.

sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD42017079261) systematic review and meta-analysis of 152 non-overlapping cohort and case-control datasets covering 98 candidate factors, with random-effects pairwise meta-analyses, correction for publication bias, sensitivity analyses, meta-regressions and a study-quality assessment. It can establish which prenatal and perinatal exposures are reliably associated with later psychosis and how large each association is. It cannot establish causation or mechanism, and because almost every individual odds ratio is small — most between 1.2 and 1.9 — it cannot support a strong single-factor neurodevelopmental claim.

sources.title: Mourning the loss of AI companions
sources.strength_why: Two natural experiments on real platform changes — Replika withdrawing erotic role play and OpenAI replacing the model behind ChatGPT — which is a design nobody can run deliberately and which the AI-and-mental-health literature otherwise lacks entirely. It CAN establish that withdrawing or altering a companion system is followed by measurable increases in negativity, loss framing and restoration desire in what users write (Replika +24.7 percentage points, 95% CI 20.1 to 29.2; ChatGPT +13.0, CI 10.8 to 15.2), with large differences in sadness (d = 2.67 vs 1.41) and self-reported negative mental health (d = 1.72 vs 0.63), and that Replika users rated closeness above common human ties (versus friend d = 0.47). It CANNOT establish how common any of this is, because the samples are self-selected forum members and survey respondents recruited from a population already attached enough to post about it, so every figure is conditional on being in that group; nor can it separate grief from the ordinary annoyance of a product change, since the comparison is between two platform changes rather than against a non-bereaved control. There is no clinical measure and no psychosis outcome. Moderate: a genuinely quasi-experimental design with confidence intervals and a very large text corpus in a strong venue, against severe selection, outcomes derived from public posts rather than instruments, and a record read from the abstract only.

sources.strength_why: A multicentre first-episode case-control study (901 cases, 1237 population controls) across 11 sites, which links individual-level exposure to site-level incidence and so does something a single-site case-control cannot: it tests whether differences in cannabis use patterns track differences in incidence between places. It can establish a graded association by frequency and potency and estimate how much of the incidence at each site is attributable to high-potency use. It cannot establish causation — the population attributable fractions are explicitly calculated 'assuming causality' — and the site-level correlations rest on only 11 data points.

sources.title: Digital phenotyping for predicting relapse in psychiatric disorders: a systematic review of passive sensing approaches.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA 2020 and SWiM systematic review of 52 passive-sensing relapse-prediction studies (4,814 participants) that applies PROBAST and reaches a usefully sceptical conclusion: 75% of studies at high risk of bias, only 10 of 52 externally validated, external validation lowering AUC by about 0.08-0.10, and not one of the 52 studies showing that deploying a prediction model improved any patient outcome. Those negative findings are the reason to hold it. It is rated INDICATIVE rather than moderate because its own reporting cannot be trusted at the level of its citations: the abstract cites 'the modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [16]' to a deep-learning paper and 'PROBAST [25, 26]' to two bipolar smartphone studies, while the body cites PROBAST as [22, 23], which are a voice-analysis paper and a circadian-phenotyping paper. Neither appraisal tool is correctly cited anywhere in the article. Add two authors from geriatrics and neurology rather than psychiatry, a three-database search excluding Embase, Scopus and Web of Science, no pooling, and a study-count table whose rows sum to 56 against 52 included studies, and the right use is as a signpost to its primary studies and as a statement of the field's validation deficit, not as an authority to be cited for a number.

sources.strength_why: A randomised trial, which is the strongest DESIGN in this part of the corpus, but an interim report on 32 participants split unevenly between arms (22 training, 10 computer-games control), with the training arm itself split 12/10 by dose. It can establish that durable cognitive gains at 6 months after neuroplasticity-based training are demonstrable and that the direction of effect favours training. It cannot establish efficacy at any useful precision: the arms are far too small, the authors describe it as interim and ongoing, and the functional-outcome improvement is explicitly non-significant. Tier is indicative, not moderate, because of sample size and interim status, not because of design. Sixteen years old, and the training software has been superseded, so it is FOUNDATIONAL for the mechanism and not current for efficacy.

sources.harvard: Folk, D., Heine, S. J. & Dunn, E. (2025) Individual differences in anthropomorphism help explain social connection to AI companions. *Scientific Reports*, 15 (1): 36548. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-19212-2 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 1274 adults recruited through Prolific Academic: Study 1, 240 US participants (mean age 38.94, SD 13.28, 55% female); Study 2, 1034 US and Canadian participants (mean age 36.61, SD 12.36, 53% female, 20% Canadian), randomised to a six-minute conversation with a ChatGPT-3.5-based chatbot or to a journaling control
sources.perspective: social psychology / two randomised online experiments with a journaling control, the second pre-registered
sources.use: Does the Nass and Moon job on 2024 data about LLMs but qualifies rather than replaces it, since the effect is d = 0.15 and larger in people already attributing mind to machines, which argues against mindless and alike.
sources.title: Individual differences in anthropomorphism help explain social connection to AI companions
sources.strength_why: Two randomised experiments, the second pre-registered and high-powered, on exactly the question Nass & Moon (2000) opened: whether people respond socially to a conversational machine. It CAN establish that a six-minute warm-prompted LLM chatbot produces more state social connection than a matched journaling control, and that the size of that gain depends on a measured individual difference — the Johnson-Neyman thresholds put 58% (Study 1) and 72% (Study 2) of participants above the point where the chatbot beat journaling, and below it there was no significant difference. It CANNOT establish that the social response is universal or mindless, which is the thing the corpus has been extending Nass & Moon to claim: the condition effect shrank from d = 0.32 to d = 0.15 in the larger study, the interaction is small (standardised 0.100, P = .013), and in Study 2 anthropomorphism predicted connection in the JOURNAL condition too (r = .310), so part of the association is not chatbot-specific at all. Also cannot bear weight on psychosis, on prolonged use, or on non-WEIRD populations: outcome is a single self-report item, exposure is six minutes, and the sample is American and Canadian Prolific workers whom the authors themselves call 'especially comfortable with technology'. Moderate rather than strong: good randomisation, pre-registration, open data and a well-chosen active control, against a one-item outcome, a brief exposure and a non-clinical convenience panel.

sources.title: Self-stigma in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 37 studies from 25 high- and low-to-middle income countries.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD42020185030) random-effects meta-analysis with no language or time restriction, pooling 37 observational studies (n=7,717) from 25 countries that used one of two validated self-stigma scales, with subgroup and meta-regression analysis of associated factors. It can establish that self-stigma is measurable and substantial across six dimensions in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, that pooled levels did not reduce over the 2007-2020 publication window, and that the correlates are social and iatrogenic (unemployment, low income, singleness, living outside urban areas, high antipsychotic dose, low functioning) rather than illness-severity indices, since psychotic severity, age at onset, illness duration, age, sex and education were NOT associated. It cannot establish direction: every included study is observational and the review reports association, so it cannot say whether stigma follows impaired functioning or helps produce it. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so no risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity statistic or funnel-plot analysis has been verified, and the pooled means are scale scores on a 1-4 range rather than an interpretable clinical threshold.

sources.title: Psychological investigation of the structure of paranoia in a non-clinical population
sources.strength_why: A large (n=1202) multidimensional questionnaire survey that established the continuum position for paranoia: the count of suspicious thoughts followed a single continuous, near-exponential distribution with no distinct subpopulation, and rarer, odder suspicions sat on top of commoner emotional concerns in a hierarchy. It can establish that paranoid thinking is common and continuously distributed in a non-clinical population and that it is structured rather than random; it cannot establish prevalence in any general population, nor causal direction, because the sample is a self-selected student convenience sample recruited by e-mail and the design is cross-sectional — both of which the authors state. Moderate rather than strong because of the sampling, not the analysis.

sources.title: Real-world comprehensive care of people living with schizophrenia: recommendations across different settings and clinical stages.
sources.strength_why: The first set of recommendations for real-world comprehensive care of schizophrenia stratified by resource setting and clinical stage, published in World Psychiatry by a 35-author panel including clinicians practising in India, South Africa, Chile, Brazil, Colombia, Uganda, Tunisia, Mexico, Malawi and Russia, with some experts by experience reviewing the materials. It can establish what the field currently recommends across eleven domains, that those recommendations differ by resource setting, and - usefully for a sceptical reading - where the authors themselves say the evidence is not yet good enough, as they do for digital monitoring technologies. It cannot establish efficacy of anything: there is no systematic search protocol, no PROSPERO registration, no formal grading of evidence, no stated number of experts and no described consensus procedure beyond 'collaborative appraisal', so it is expert opinion built on a critical review and must be cited as a recommendation rather than as evidence. Rated moderate on venue, breadth, transparency about its own uncertainty and the inclusion of non-Western practice, and held below strong by the absence of any stated method for either the search or the consensus.

sources.title: Factors associated with aggressive behavior in patients with schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD420251147415), PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis searching ten databases, six English and four Chinese (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, CBM), 2014 to October 2024, with Newcastle-Ottawa quality scoring (mostly 7-9 of 9), sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and funnel plots. It can establish the strength of association between a defined set of correlates and aggression in people already diagnosed with schizophrenia, with pooled odds ratios and confidence intervals. It cannot establish causation or anything about the onset of psychosis: the authors state that the included studies were 'primarily case-control and cross-sectional studies, which limit causal inference regarding etiology', and the outcome 'aggressive behavior' had no standardised operational definition across the primary studies. Current, not foundational. Fit caveat, which matters more here than the tier: this is violence risk in established schizophrenia, a different construct and a different population from first-episode or clinical high-risk psychosis, so it cannot carry any predisposing-factor claim in Essay 1.

sources.title: Evidence-based interventions for vocational recovery in first-episode psychosis: A meta-analysis of employment and education rates.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered PRISMA meta-analysis of 31 studies (n=8,651) with formal risk-of-bias assessment (RoB2 and ROBINS-E) and GRADE certainty rating, analysing employment, education and combined vocational rates both as pooled proportions and as intervention-versus-control comparisons. It can establish that vocational intervention improves competitive employment after a first episode (overall OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.88-2.94; Individual Placement and Support OR 2.86, 95% CI 1.81-4.54) and - the more useful half for this project - that no intervention showed a consistent advantage for EDUCATION rates, with a confidence interval that includes no effect (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.80-1.76). It cannot establish much about the combined endpoint, which the authors themselves describe as limited in interpretability by substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 69.6%, tau-squared 0.296, p<0.001) and possible publication bias. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so the GRADE certainty ratings, the per-outcome risk-of-bias judgements, the countries of included studies and the definitions of 'education' are all unverified, and because an online-first record carries no volume, issue or page numbers.

sources.population: 11867 participants from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, a longitudinal population-based cohort recruited at ages 9-10 across 21 sites in the United States, with psychotic-like-experience data at more than one timepoint; screen time taken from Year 2 (ages approximately 11-12) and the outcome from Year 4 (ages approximately 13-14)

sources.title: Trajectories of distressing psychotic-like experience in youth: the interplay of recent negative life events and screen time
sources.strength_why: The only source found that puts adversity and digital media in the same prospective model with a psychosis-relevant outcome, which is exactly where the corpus's trauma strand and its technology strand fail to meet. Its strength is not uniform and should not be cited as if it were. The TRAJECTORY findings are moderate and rest on the full cohort: latent growth mixture modelling over five timepoints in 11867 ABCD participants gave an increasing PLE-distress class (n=409), a decreasing class (n=698) and a no-distress class (n=10759), and youth in the increasing class reported more recent negative life events while reporting similar total daily screen time to the decreasing class — so adversity, not screen volume, is what separates the two symptomatic trajectories. The MODERATION findings, which are the ones an essay would actually want, are indicative at best: the weekend screen time x negative life events interaction (B 0.51, SE 0.19, t 2.74, P=.007, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.86) comes from a mixed model with n=103, the weekday equivalent was NOT significant (P=.12), and the texting and social-media results the abstract leads with are labelled exploratory in the body and carry t(90). It CANNOT establish that screen use causes PLE distress, cannot speak to AI or chatbots at all, and its 4-year outcome data were released for only around 40% of the cohort with the increasing-distress trajectory differentially under-represented. Moderate overall, with the carve-out stated.

sources.title: Neurobiology of early life adversity: A systematic review of meta-analyses towards an integrative account of its neurobiological trajectories to mental disorders.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 27 meta-analyses that can establish convergent neurobiological correlates of adverse childhood experiences across four previously separate literatures — HPA axis, inflammation, neuroimaging and genetics/epigenetics — and can establish that those correlates appear in people with and without a psychiatric diagnosis, which is a real and unusual finding. It cannot establish causation and the authors call for longitudinal work to do so; it is also a review of reviews, so it is three steps from any participant and inherits every constituent meta-analysis's bias. Its outcome is mental disorders in general, NOT psychosis, which limits its fit here. Tier is moderate: rigorous method, stated limitations, but an umbrella design on a non-specific outcome.

sources.title: Psychological mechanisms mediating effects between trauma and psychotic symptoms: the role of affect regulation, intrusive trauma memory, beliefs, and depression
sources.strength_why: The best source found for the proposition that childhood adversity is associated with the TYPE of psychotic symptom and not only with risk or severity, and it is a clinical sample of 228 people with relapsing psychosis rather than a student or community survey. It CAN establish specificity in this sample: childhood emotional abuse was associated with persecutory and referential delusions while childhood sexual abuse was associated with auditory hallucinations, and the persecutory association was statistically mediated by negative beliefs about other people. It CANNOT establish temporal order or cause, and the authors say so themselves — 'The study was cross-sectional and future work should investigate these processes in prospective or longitudinal studies'; trauma was recalled retrospectively by people who already had psychosis, PTSD symptoms were self-reported rather than interviewed, and the mediation models for hallucinations rest on n = 118 complete cases, not 228. Moderate rather than strong: a well-specified a priori hypothesis set with a counterfactual mediation framework and a representativeness check against trial non-completers, against a cross-sectional design, retrospective recall, and a symptom coding that collapses 0-5 severity scales to present/absent.

sources.title: Predicting PANSS symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorders using speech only: an international, multi-centre, retrospective, computational study across multiple languages.
sources.strength_why: A medRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Version 1 was posted 28 February 2026 and version 2 on 30 September 2026; the medRxiv API returns `published: NA` for both as of 12 October 2026, so no journal version exists to cite instead. Under this project's appraisal tiers a preprint is not-citable where a peer-reviewed alternative exists, and for the specific question it answers - item-level PANSS prediction from speech alone across ten languages - no peer-reviewed alternative exists at all, which is why it is filed rather than discarded. Judged on publication status, not on method: the method as described is strong for its genre (speaker-disjoint splits, 16 algorithms compared per item, bias checks by age, sex, education and severity, models released), and the authors' own stated limitation is that the dataset is heterogeneous in samples, languages, symptom assessment and speech elicitation. Nothing from it may enter the essays as evidence. It may be mentioned as a preprint, with that word attached, or used to locate the primary site studies it pooled.

sources.title: Longitudinal bidirectional relationships between problematic smartphone use and psychotic-like experiences among young adults: the mediating role of excessive daytime sleepiness
sources.strength_why: The only prospective study found anywhere on a technology the corpus's argument is actually about: smartphone use and psychotic-like experiences, three waves at six-month intervals, 6153 young adults, with within-person modelling that separates change in a person from differences between people. It CAN establish temporal order in this sample, and the order runs the way the argument does not want: after accounting for stable between-person differences the random-intercept model 'provided no evidence for a bidirectional association', and the surviving within-person path was increases in psychotic-like experiences at Time 1 predicting increases in problematic smartphone use at Time 3 through daytime sleepiness at Time 2. It CANNOT establish anything about generative AI, chatbots or conversational agents — the exposure is problematic smartphone use as a global construct — nor about diagnosed psychosis, since the outcome is self-reported psychotic-like experiences in a non-clinical student sample. Moderate rather than strong: a large, genuinely prospective, within-person design with the right comparison of CLPM against RI-CLPM, against entirely self-reported exposure and outcome, an 79.7% female sample, a single-country single-population frame, and a record read from the abstract only, so no effect sizes, intervals or attrition have been checked.

sources.title: Association between cannabis use disorder and schizophrenia stronger in young males than in females.
sources.strength_why: A nationwide register cohort covering 6,907,859 people and 129,521,260 person-years with 45,327 incident schizophrenia cases, which effectively removes selection and recall bias from exposure and outcome measurement and is large enough to estimate sex- and age-stratified effects and population attributable fractions over fifty years. It can establish that the association between diagnosed cannabis use disorder and schizophrenia is graded by sex and age and has grown over time. It cannot establish causation, and the exposure is a recorded diagnosis of cannabis use disorder rather than cannabis use, so it captures the severe tail of use and nothing below it.

sources.harvard: Howes, O. D. & Kapur, S. (2009) The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: version III - the final common pathway. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 35 (3): 549-562. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbp006 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no recruited participants - a selective review synthesising five streams of evidence (neurochemical imaging, genetics, environmental risk factors, the extended phenotype, animal studies) drawn from over 6700 articles on dopamine and schizophrenia
sources.perspective: molecular psychiatry and PET neurochemical imaging / selective synthesis across five evidence streams into a causal framework
sources.use: Its second contribution matters more than the dopamine figures: aberrant salience filtered through existing cognitive and sociocultural schemas is the joint between a brain account and Essay 2's content-shaping argument, stated by the field's canonical paper.
sources.title: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: version III--the final common pathway
sources.strength_why: The field's canonical statement of the current dopamine hypothesis, peer reviewed in Schizophrenia Bulletin, open access, and the paper that explicitly ties dopamine dysfunction to psychotic experience through aberrant salience - the mechanism `notes/bokhari-2026-technology-delusions.md` already leans on without the corpus holding a primary for it. It can establish what the hypothesis now claims, that elevated presynaptic striatal dopamine synthesis capacity is the most widely replicated dopaminergic abnormality in schizophrenia with reported effect sizes of 0.63 to 1.89 across seven of nine studies, that striatal dopamine elevation is absent in mania, depression and non-psychotic psychiatric disorders, and that the authors locate the abnormality with **psychosis** rather than with schizophrenia as a diagnosis. It cannot establish causation, direction or sequence: it is a selective review of cross-sectional case-control PET studies, the measures are indirect indices rather than dopamine levels, and the authors say the hypothesis 'will be revised as more data become available'. Moderate rather than strong because it is a selective narrative synthesis with no stated search strategy or risk-of-bias assessment, and because the imaging evidence it rests on is almost entirely small-sample - see the appraisal against Marek et al. below.

sources.title: Delusional Experiences Emerging From AI Chatbot Interactions or 'AI Psychosis'
sources.strength_why: A peer-reviewed Viewpoint in JMIR Mental Health that defines AI psychosis as a heuristic framework rather than a diagnostic entity and maps it onto the stress-vulnerability model, the digital therapeutic alliance and theory-of-mind accounts. It can establish how the term is used in the published literature and supply a conceptual vocabulary for a mechanism; it cannot establish that the mechanism operates, how often, or in whom, because it reports no data and the authors state the pathways are heuristic and make no causal claim. Indicative rather than weak because it is peer reviewed, explicitly scoped, and the authors are psychiatrists writing within established psychosis models, but it remains opinion rather than evidence.

sources.title: M6W4 – Evidence-Based Treatments for Complex Mental Health Conditions
sources.strength_why: Course teaching slides, unattributed to a named author, not peer reviewed and not publicly retrievable, so it cannot be cited as evidence for any claim in either essay — citing it would also be citing course notes, which the Module 3 brief explicitly asks students to distinguish from their own ideas and to reference properly. Its value is entirely as a SPECIFICATION of what the marker expects: it fixes the course's own wording of the 5Ps, of holistic formulation and of Verstehen, and it names the psychosis treatment list the assessment assumes. Every substantive point it makes must be re-sourced to a primary or secondary publication before it enters the essay. Tier is not-citable by definition of the venue, not by any defect in the content.

sources.title: Enhancing neuroplasticity to augment cognitive remediation in schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A short mini-review, team-independent of the Vinogradov lineage, that can establish that response to cognitive remediation is highly variable, that combining it with exercise or tDCS is a live research strategy, and that the mechanistic rationale runs through BDNF and long-term potentiation. It cannot establish that the combination works: the authors state there are 'insufficient data to determine if this multimodal approach leads to incremental performance gain in patients' and call for larger RCTs. Nine years old and the tDCS literature has grown substantially since, so any claim about the state of that evidence must be dated. Tier is indicative: a mini-review with no primary data and explicitly insufficient evidence on its own question.

sources.title: Cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis with examination of potential bias
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 52 randomised trials, pre-specified moderator analyses for three Cochrane risk-of-bias domains plus use of a control intervention, and three separate publication-bias tests: it is the primary source for every effect size the 2019 editorial reports, and it is the strongest treatment-efficacy source now in the corpus. It establishes that pooled end-of-treatment effects of CBT on overall, positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia lie in the small range and that masking of outcome assessment significantly moderates them, with positive symptoms falling to non-significance in masked trials. Its own stated limits are real: the low-risk-of-bias subanalyses rest on 8-11 studies because most trials were rated 'unclear' rather than low or high risk, and it did not examine effects on depression, anxiety or distress, so it can say nothing about those. Full appraisal from the full text; strong on design and directly on the claim.

sources.title: CBT for schizophrenia: a critical viewpoint
sources.strength_why: An editorial 'critical viewpoint', not an independent synthesis: it reports effect sizes drawn from other meta-analyses, one of which is the authors' own (Jauhar et al., 2014), and it has no protocol, no search strategy and no risk-of-bias assessment of its own. It can establish that the pooled effect of CBTp on positive symptoms in meta-analyses published since 2014 lies in the small range, that the effect attenuates under blinding, and that these authors read the evidence as not supporting CBTp for negative symptoms or relapse prevention. It cannot stand as the source of an effect-size figure, because every number in it is secondary; for those, cite Jauhar et al. (2014), British Journal of Psychiatry, 204 (1): 20-29, directly. Indicative rather than moderate because of the publication type and the authors' declared position in the controversy.

sources.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy plus standard care versus standard care plus other psychosocial treatments for people with schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review with a registered protocol, a specialist trials register searched without language or publication-status limits, independent duplicate screening and extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE rating: the strongest design in the corpus for a treatment question. What it establishes is narrow and often misread: it compares CBT against OTHER psychosocial therapies as add-ons, not against standard care alone, and it found no clear difference on relapse, rehospitalisation, mental state, death, social functioning or quality of life. It therefore cannot be cited for the size of CBTp's effect against treatment-as-usual, and the authors themselves rate the evidence as mainly low or very low quality. Strong on design; the fit to the claim it is currently being used for is poor.

sources.title: International incidence of psychotic disorders, 2002-17: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review (CRD42018086800) screening 56,721 records to 177 included studies, with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression that tests study method as an explanation for the variation it finds. It can establish the pooled incidence of psychotic disorders, the size of the male and ethnic-minority excess, and that part of the geographical variation is an artefact of case-ascertainment design. It cannot establish causes, and heterogeneity was extreme (I-squared at or above 98.5%), which means the pooled rate of 26.6 per 100,000 person-years is a summary of a very dispersed distribution rather than a figure that describes any particular place.

sources.title: Psychosis as a state of aberrant salience: a framework linking biology, phenomenology, and pharmacology in schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: The primary source for aberrant salience: the paper that proposed dopamine's role as mediating the salience of events and representations, and that delusions are the person's own cognitive effort to make sense of aberrantly salient experience while hallucinations are the direct experience of aberrant salience in internal representations. It can establish what the framework claims and where it came from, which is what the corpus needs, because the mechanism is currently cited through `notes/bokhari-2026-technology-delusions.md` and restated in `notes/howes-2009-dopamine-hypothesis-iii.md`. It cannot establish anything empirically: it collects no data, tests nothing, and the author describes it as 'a heuristic framework' and discusses its limitations himself. Indicative is the tier for a theory paper used for a concept - it is foundational and it is not evidence, and no amount of citation makes a framework a finding. Rated from the abstract and from Howes and Kapur's (2009) restatement of it; the full text is paywalled.

sources.strength_why: A theoretical synthesis, not a study: it can establish that a coherent 'dysplastic' model exists in the peer-reviewed literature and can supply the critical-period vocabulary for discussing when risk converts to onset, but it cannot evidence any individual causal link, because every empirical claim in it is a secondary citation. The tier is indicative because it is a theory paper by authors with authority in the field, with no primary data of its own.

sources.title: Social deprivation, inequality, and the neighborhood-level incidence of psychotic syndromes in East London.
sources.strength_why: A population-based first-episode incidence study using Bayesian hierarchical models with spatially structured neighbourhood random effects, which is the appropriate design for this question, and it separates three correlated exposures that are usually confounded: income inequality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.04-1.49 per SD), absolute deprivation (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.08-1.51) and population density (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.00-1.41), each independently associated with non-affective psychosis after standardising for individual age, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic status. It is the only source in the corpus in which deprivation predicts PSYCHOSIS rather than general psychopathology, which is precisely the hole in `e1-predispose`. It CANNOT establish causation, and cannot separate social causation from social drift — people with emerging psychosis may move into deprived areas. The density interval reaches 1.00, no neighbourhood-level variation was found for the AFFECTIVE psychoses, and it is a single city over two years with 427 cases, so the neighbourhood-level estimates rest on small numbers per area.

sources.title: 'People don't understand': An investigation of stigma in schizophrenia using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA)
sources.strength_why: An early interpretative phenomenological analysis whose stated purpose was 'to provide an account of the life experiences of persons with schizophrenia', which is the kind of evidence this corpus is thinnest on, and which generated super-ordinate themes of judgement, comparison and personal understanding, with stigma appearing as both public stigma and self-stigma. It can indicate how a small number of people with a schizophrenia diagnosis described being judged and judging themselves, and it is the earliest qualitative account of psychosis the corpus holds. It cannot establish how common any of that is, and it cannot speak to onset, first episode or risk at all - stigma is the phenomenon, not psychosis. Indicative rather than moderate on three counts: six participants; no full text read, so the sampling, analytic rigour and reflexivity are entirely unverified; and the abstract reports no recruitment setting, no country, no age range and no illness duration, so there is no way to judge who these six people were.

sources.title: Antipsychotic treatment, psychoeducation & regular follow up as a public health strategy for schizophrenia: results from a prospective study.
sources.strength_why: A prospective community cohort in rural south India reporting that 70.6% (95% CI 64.35-76.95) achieved clinical remission and 69.6% (95% CI 63.29-76.07) a satisfactory outcome after about four years of ensured continuous antipsychotics plus low-intensity psychoeducation, with disability falling from 66.7% to 27.3% of the cohort. It is valuable as one of very few sources combining pharmacological and educational components in a non-Western population, and the authors' framing — that a minority need structured psychosocial work beyond this — is a usable qualification. It CANNOT support an efficacy claim: there is no control group, no randomisation and no comparison period, so remission cannot be attributed to the intervention rather than to natural course, regression to the mean or ascertainment; the two components are bundled and cannot be separated; n = 201 in one taluk; and the published abstract is garbled at the disability p-value ('PInterpretation'), so that statistic is NOT recorded here. Indicative because the design cannot carry more.

sources.population: 55 consecutively first-admitted inpatients aged 16-65 (43 men, 12 women; mean age 25, range 16-40) at the Regional Unit of Psychosis, Nordland Hospital, Bodo, Northern Norway, admitted between 1 August 2014 and 1 August 2016; catchment population 480,000

sources.use: Lets the intake question be asked properly rather than assumed, since a fully structured self-report protocol standardised the questions and lost over half the schizophrenia-spectrum cases, in exactly the first-presentation population the vignette belongs to.
sources.title: Does method matter? Assessing the validity and clinical utility of structured diagnostic interviews among a clinical sample of first-admitted patients with psychosis: A replication study.
sources.strength_why: A naturalistic replication in a consecutive, catchment-based first-admission psychosis sample, comparing SCID-I/P diagnoses made by a trained non-clinician against best-estimate consensus diagnoses assigned by a multidisciplinary team using all available information, with kappa, sensitivity and specificity and a cross-tabulation reported in full. It can establish that in this real clinical setting a fully structured interview agreed poorly with the consensus standard (kappa 0.21), missed 24 of 44 schizophrenia-spectrum cases, and generated two or more comorbid diagnoses in 49% of patients, and it can establish that this replicates an earlier independent finding (Nordgaard et al., kappa 0.18). It cannot establish that structured interviews are invalid in general: n=55, one interviewer, one specialist unit, a non-random sample enriched for schizophrenia-spectrum presentations, and a protocol deliberately administered in a fully structured way without medical-record review, which the SCID User's Guide does not require. Rated moderate: a sound primary study with high ecological validity and limitations the authors state plainly, not a design that can carry a general claim.

sources.strength_why: An individually matched case-control study nested in a population-based incidence programme, with cases ascertained by SCAN and exposure measured by the WHO ASSIST, which can establish that cannabis use was more common in cases than matched controls in each setting and that in Trinidad the association was graded by frequency and dependence. It cannot establish temporal order or causation, and in India and Nigeria cannabis use was too rare for any association to be estimated at all, so the paper supports no conclusion about those two settings. Moderate rather than strong because the design is cross-sectional in exposure and several Trinidad confidence intervals are wide or include 1.

sources.title: Feasibility, acceptability and clinical utility of the Cultural Formulation Interview: mixed-methods results from the DSM-5 international field trial.
sources.strength_why: A mixed-methods field trial across 14 sites in six countries, with 318 patients and 75 clinicians, which is the evidential basis on which the Cultural Formulation Interview was adopted into DSM-5; it can establish that a structured cultural assessment is feasible, acceptable and seen as clinically useful in routine practice, and it is the one source here with substantial non-Western and Global South participants (Kenya, India, Peru) rather than non-Western authors. It CANNOT establish that cultural formulation improves clinical outcomes: the outcomes are feasibility, acceptability and perceived utility, there is no control condition, and the paper reports that clinician feasibility ratings were significantly LOWER than patients', improving only after the first administration. Moderate rather than strong because the design is an implementation field trial without a comparator and because 'clinical utility' here is a rating, not an outcome.

sources.title: Psychosen

Not-citable in the sense the tier intends: for an English-language MSc essay it is unverifiable by the reader and by the marker, and using it would mean citing a secondary synthesis in a language the essay is not written in for a claim that empirical sources can carry directly. The entry exists so that the chain is documented, not so that the book is cited.

sources.title: A systematic review and discussion of symptom specific cognitive behavioural approaches to delusions and hallucinations
sources.strength_why: A systematic review of RCTs published in a specialist journal, which can establish that the small number of trials of symptom-specific CBT for delusions or hallucinations have reported post-therapy effect sizes above d=0.4 on at least one primary outcome, and that this compares favourably with the small-to-moderate range reported for generic CBTp. It cannot establish efficacy, because by the authors' own account only three of twelve trials were adequately powered, the rest were pilots, no meta-analytic pooling or risk-of-bias assessment is reported in the abstract, and follow-up periods were mostly brief. Moderate rather than strong on that basis, and because the record is abstract-only - no pooled estimate, no heterogeneity and no publication-bias check has been inspected.

Available from: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1381864 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 33 primary studies of clinical (help-seeking) samples assessed for both clinical high risk for psychosis and borderline personality pathology; adolescents and young adults in specialist early-intervention and inpatient services
sources.perspective: clinical psychology and youth early-intervention psychiatry / PRISMA-ScR scoping review with narrative synthesis
sources.use: Describes what the clinical-high-risk state actually is - subthreshold, help-seeking and functionally impaired rather than a diagnosis, which is an e1-what point about the continuum - and the live argument it documents over whether that risk is psychosis-specific or pluripotent is what makes e1-assess point that a positive screen says less than it appears to.
sources.title: Harmonizing early intervention strategies: scoping review of clinical high risk for psychosis and borderline personality disorder.
sources.strength_why: A pre-registered (OSF 8mz7a), PRISMA-ScR/JBI-compliant scoping review of three databases to August 2023, with independent dual title/abstract and full-text screening and third-judge adjudication, mapping 33 primary studies into four clinical-research paradigms. It can establish what the clinical high-risk literature actually measures and with which instruments (CAARMS, SIPS, SPI-A, ERIraos), that CHR-P is operationalised as a help-seeking, subthreshold, functionally impaired state rather than a diagnosis, and that transdiagnostic 'clinical staging' and 'pluripotency' models (CHARMS) are now competing with the psychosis-specific risk paradigm. It cannot establish prevalence, effect size or any causal claim: a scoping review by design does not appraise the quality of the studies it maps or pool their results, and the authors state as their first limitation that 'our study design did not allow for the development of clinical guidelines'. Treated as current rather than foundational: published June 2024, searched to August 2023.

sources.title: Mindfulness- and acceptance-based interventions for psychosis: our current understanding and a meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of third-wave (mindfulness, acceptance and compassion) interventions in psychosis, with psychotic symptoms as the pre-specified primary outcome and subgroup analysis separating group mindfulness-based work from individual ACT. It establishes that a usable randomised evidence base for mindfulness in psychosis EXISTS, and that its pooled effect on symptoms is small: g = 0.29 overall, with g = 0.46 for group mindfulness-based interventions and g = 0.08 for individual ACT-based ones. It cannot carry more than that: only 10 trials were pooled, there were no significant effects on positive symptoms, negative symptoms, hallucination distress or functioning, the authors state that further research is needed to determine the efficacy of specific treatment models, and the paper is closed access so the forest plots, risk-of-bias table and trial countries have NOT been read. Moderate rather than strong on the small number of trials, the null secondary outcomes and the abstract-only basis.

sources.title: Affecting coping: does neurocognition predict approach and avoidant coping strategies within schizophrenia spectrum disorders?
sources.strength_why: A single-site cross-sectional group comparison with a small clinical cell (27 patients) and a schizotypy group three times its size, read from the abstract only. It can establish an association between trait affect and self-reported coping style across schizophrenia-spectrum groups, and it reports that neurocognition did not predict coping style - a null result the authors did not expect. It cannot establish that coping ability causes or precedes symptom exacerbation, because nothing in it is longitudinal and symptom exacerbation is not an outcome it measures. Indicative because of the design, the cell sizes and abstract-only access.

sources.title: Is diagnosis enough to guide interventions in mental health? Using case formulation in clinical practice.
sources.strength_why: This is the citable peer-reviewed statement of the Five Ps framework, and it sets out all five headings — presenting problem, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective/positive factors — with worked clinical content under each. It can establish what the framework is, what each P is meant to contain, and that it is one approach among several rather than a validated instrument; the authors call it 'one of the more popular recent approaches', so it is a description of practice, not a derivation. It CANNOT establish that formulation improves outcomes: it is a debate and commentary piece with no data, no participants and no systematic search, and the authors themselves say research on the impact of formulation on outcome 'is still somewhat limited'. Indicative rather than moderate for that reason — the tier reflects the design, not the fit, which for `e2-plan` is excellent.

sources.title: Meta-analysis of the Association Between the Level of Cannabis Use and Risk of Psychosis.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review of 571 references down to 18 studies, with 10 pooled by a random-effects method that simulates individual data points from the published summary data in order to fit a dose-response model, across 66,816 individuals. It can establish a graded association between level of cannabis use and psychosis risk, with an odds ratio of 3.90 (95% CI 2.84-5.34) for the heaviest users against non-users. It cannot establish causation and the authors say so explicitly, and the simulation step means the dose-response curve is reconstructed from summary data rather than observed, which is a real inferential cost.

sources.population: pooled secondary analysis of three community-recruited neuroimaging cohorts: ABCD (n=11,874 recruited, 3,928 after motion censoring; aged 9-10; 21 US sites), Human Connectome Project (n=1,200 recruited, 900 used; aged 22-35; single US site), UK Biobank (n=35,735 recruited, 32,572 used; aged 40-69; UK)

sources.title: Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals
sources.strength_why: Peer-reviewed in Nature, open access, with named reviewers, open code and open data, and it uses the three largest neuroimaging datasets in existence (~50,000 people) rather than arguing from theory, so it can establish how large a sample a brain-wide association study needs before its effect sizes stop being inflated. It can establish that median univariate brain-behaviour effects are |r| = 0.01, that the largest effect replicating out of sample was |r| = 0.16, that at n = 25 the 99% confidence interval spans r +/- 0.52, and that at n < 500 replication rates were around 5%. It cannot establish anything about any specific disorder, it is cross-sectional and observational throughout, and the authors are explicit that it does NOT condemn small-sample neuroimaging in general — within-person, lesion and intervention designs have larger effects and are exempt. Several authors declare a financial interest in NOUS Imaging Inc., disclosed and managed. Tier is strong: adequately powered by construction, directly on the methodological claim, with the authors' own scope limits stated.

sources.title: 'I'm ruined': Young people's and their mothers' experiences of living with, and receiving a diagnosis of, borderline personality disorder: An interpretative phenomenological analysis
sources.strength_why: A sound primary qualitative study: IPA following the Smith, Flowers and Larkin six-step procedure, a genuinely novel multi-perspectival dyadic design, research-supervision triangulation of codes and themes, NHS research ethics approval, and participants offered sight of their transcripts to withdraw material - four did. It can establish what living with and being labelled with a borderline personality disorder diagnosis is like for a small number of English adolescents and their mothers. **It is not about psychosis**, and it cannot carry any claim about psychotic experience, onset or first episode. Moderate on its own terms; the reason it is not useful here is fit, not quality, which is why `serves` is empty.

sources.title: The economic impact of early intervention in psychosis services for children and adolescents.
sources.strength_why: A transparent decision model with a sensitivity analysis that can establish that early intervention in psychosis for under-18s plausibly produces short-term direct healthcare savings, driven by reduced in-patient length of stay, and that the base-case result was robust to varying each parameter by 50%. It cannot establish clinical effectiveness, because it measures cost and not outcome, and it is a model rather than a trial — the authors say so: 'like trials, decision models represent simplifications of reality'. Its cost figures are 2009-11 UK prices and are therefore fifteen years out of date as money, though the direction of the argument survives. Tier is moderate: sound method, stated limitations, single-region data, non-clinical outcome.

sources.title: Loneliness in psychosis: a meta-analytical review.
sources.strength_why: A random-effects meta-analysis of 13 studies and 15 647 participants with study and outcome quality assessed using adapted AHRQ and GRADE tools, finding a moderate association between loneliness and psychotic symptoms (r = .32, 95% CI 0.20-0.44) that did not depend on whether loneliness was measured by a single item or a full scale — a measurement-robustness check that matters, because the single-item objection is the obvious one. It can establish that loneliness and psychotic symptoms covary at a clinically meaningful magnitude, which is what lets social isolation be treated as a target rather than a backdrop. It CANNOT establish direction or cause: the authors say explicitly that 'further studies are needed to determine the causal status of this relationship', the included studies are correlational, and heterogeneity is extreme at I-squared = 97.56%, so the pooled r of .32 summarises a very dispersed set of estimates. The authors rate their own evidence 'moderate quality'.

sources.title: Epidemiology of Untreated Psychoses in 3 Diverse Settings in the Global South: The International Research Program on Psychotic Disorders in Diverse Settings (INTREPID II).
sources.strength_why: A population-based incidence study over 3,790,697 person-years in three Global South catchment areas, using identical instruments (SCAN, PPHS) and case-finding across the professional, folk and popular sectors, with leakage studies and interrater reliability reported. It can establish that rates and the demographic and clinical shape of psychosis vary markedly by setting, and that the Global North sex-and-age pattern does not hold everywhere. It cannot establish incidence in the strict sense — the outcome is rate of *untreated* psychosis, a proxy — and the authors say rates where duration of untreated psychosis is long, as in Kancheepuram, are the least accurate proxies.

sources.title: Artificial intelligence-associated delusions and large language models: risks, mechanisms of delusion co-creation, and safeguarding strategies.
sources.strength_why: A Lancet Psychiatry Personal View, which is a high-visibility venue but an opinion format: no systematic search, no participants, no data of its own. It can establish three things that matter and that no study in the corpus establishes as crisply: that the current evidence indicates reinforcement of existing delusional beliefs rather than induction of de novo psychosis in the absence of vulnerability; that benefit and harm are both on the table, the AI agent sometimes functioning as 'a benign and predictable conversational anchor'; and that the proposed safeguards are UNTESTED, because the authors themselves say the protocols 'must be urgently co-designed with service users and clinicians and tested in clinical trials'. It CANNOT establish prevalence, mechanism or efficacy of anything, and its proposed framework of AI-informed care is a proposal. Indicative on design; its fit to `e2-mechanism`, `e2-evidence` and the education strand of `e2-plan` is excellent.

sources.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Adolescent Mental Health
sources.strength_why: A densely referenced 2026 narrative review in a peer-reviewed paediatrics journal, open access, which can establish what the current literature on adolescent generative AI use and mental health consists of, organise it by disorder, and supply the mechanisms the field is proposing - problematic and dependent use, sycophancy from reinforcement learning from human feedback, anthropomorphism, compensatory use, social displacement and cognitive offloading. Its most citable contribution is a limitation it states repeatedly in its own voice: the evidence is 'predominantly cross-sectional', consists 'predominantly of cross-sectional studies, case reports, and self-reported data, limiting the ability to establish temporality or causality', and the relationships 'may be bidirectional'. It cannot establish any association itself, because it conducts no analysis, and - the reason it is not rated moderate - it describes itself as a narrative review and **states no search strategy, no databases, no date range and no inclusion criteria**, so what it left out is unknowable.

sources.title: Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management. NICE clinical guideline CG178.
sources.strength_why: A national clinical guideline developed through NICE's published process: commissioned systematic reviews, a multidisciplinary committee including service users and carers, consultation, and dated versioning with an audit trail of what changed and when. For the question 'what should a care plan for psychosis contain, and on whose authority', nothing outranks it in a UK context, and it is the document a UK marker will expect a holistic plan to be measured against. It establishes the expected SHAPE of care - oral antipsychotic plus family intervention and individual CBT at first episode, crisis resolution and home treatment as the first-line crisis service, supported employment, physical health monitoring, carer support, peer support and self-management - and it does so at the level of detail a 500-word plan can actually use. It establishes NOTHING about whether any of those interventions works: it is a consensus synthesis, so its recommendations are a committee's judgement on evidence, not evidence, and several load-bearing recommendations are marked [2009], meaning their last evidence review was in 2009. Essay 2 may cite it for what a plan should include and must not cite it for efficacy.
