sources.title: Rehabilitation for adults with complex psychosis. NICE guideline NG181.
sources.strength_why: A national guideline developed through NICE's documented process, with named evidence reviews cited against each recommendation group (reviews A, C, E, F, G, I and P), covering a territory CG178 barely touches: rehabilitation pathways, supported accommodation, structured daily and group activity, supported employment, and team formulation. For the question 'what does rehabilitation actually consist of, and on whose authority', it is the UK authority and the only source in this corpus that addresses housing at all. It establishes the expected CONTENT of a rehabilitation and recovery plan - supported accommodation, daily living skills, structured group social and leisure activity, IPS-model supported employment, recovery colleges, and mindfulness among the additional psychological interventions - at a level a short plan can cite in one go. It establishes NOTHING about efficacy: it is a consensus synthesis, and it is scoped to COMPLEX psychosis, meaning treatment-resistant symptoms with impaired functioning, so it is the wrong citation for a first-episode or recent-onset case without saying so explicitly.

sources.population: 16 members of an epidemiologically complete first-episode psychosis incidence cohort (n=171) in an urban catchment area in Ireland, interviewed circa 21 years after their FEP; mean age 26.94 (SD 8.32) at FEP onset and 47.68 (SD 8.34) at interview; 11 (68.75%) male, all 16 (100%) Caucasian

sources.title: Meaning in Life in Long-Term Recovery in First-Episode Psychosis: An Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis
sources.strength_why: A sound primary qualitative study: IPA conducted inside an epidemiologically complete FEP incidence cohort, with purposive maximum-variation sampling deliberately balanced across remission status, age at onset and gender, Yardley's four quality criteria applied and documented action by action, three analysis phases, personal and epistemological reflexivity reported, and the authors' own limitations stated at length. It answers what recovery and meaning are like from the service user's own standpoint two decades after a first episode - a question no outcome scale in this corpus asks - and it supplies an operational definition of first-episode psychosis and the remission criteria the cohort used. It cannot establish how common any of these experiences is, nor how meaning is experienced soon after onset, because every account is retrospective by about 21 years and the authors name recall bias themselves. Moderate rather than strong: 16 people, all Caucasian, mostly male, mostly unemployed, with possible recruitment bias towards those already interested in meaning in life, and the sample was not balanced across baseline diagnoses.

sources.strength_why: A sound primary neuroimaging study that can establish that, within a psychosis population, those additionally meeting ICD-11 cPTSD criteria differ structurally in limbic and prefrontal regions — larger bilateral anterior insula and left parahippocampus, smaller left medial orbitofrontal cortex — with all differences bar hippocampal volume surviving whole-brain correction. Antipsychotic and other psychotropic exposure is a stated confounder and differed between groups. Tier is moderate, not strong: n=108 across two separately acquired samples on three different scanners, with correlational post-hoc analyses described by the authors only as trends.

sources.title: Trajectories of Adolescent Media Use and Their Associations With Psychotic Experiences.
sources.strength_why: The only genuinely prospective source in this corpus on digital media use and psychotic experiences: a population birth cohort followed from 5 months to 23 years, with exposure reported at ages 12, 13, 15 and 17 and the outcome measured at 23, so the temporal order is fixed by design rather than by recall, and with adjustment for sociodemographic, genetic, family and childhood covariables measured between 5 months and 12 years. It can establish that adolescent media-use trajectories are at most MODESTLY associated with psychotic experiences in young adulthood, and - more usefully - that part of what looks like an effect is confounding by prior mental health: higher video gaming 'was preceded by higher levels of mental health and interpersonal problems at age 12 years', and adjusting for those 'mitigated the association'. It CANNOT support any claim about generative AI, smartphones or social media: the four exposures are television viewing, video gaming, computer use and reading, reported in a cohort born 1997-1998, so the exposure window is roughly 2010 to 2015 and predates the technology Essay 2 is about. Only ONE association survived adjustment - a curved trajectory of computer use, n=189 - and the authors' own conclusion attributes the findings 'likely' to shared risk factors. Strong on design; the fit to an AI claim is poor and must be stated.

sources.use: The strongest intervention evidence for anything resembling the vignette's reframing need, with its largest effect on delusions specifically and holding a year, though the effect on reasoning biases is small, so the mechanism is its weakest part.
sources.title: Immediate and sustained outcomes and moderators associated with metacognitive training for psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-reported meta-analysis of 43 studies, searching eleven databases from 2007 to June 2021, pooling 1816 participants and reporting Hedges g with 95% confidence intervals for proximal and distal outcomes, with effects maintained up to one year. It can establish that a structured intervention aimed at reasoning and cognitive biases reduces delusions (g = 0.69, 95% CI 0.45-0.93) and positive symptoms (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.67) — a directly targeted, durable effect on the symptom class the vignette turns on. It CANNOT establish that it works by changing cognitive biases: the effect on cognitive biases themselves is the smallest significant one in the paper (g = 0.16, 95% CI 0.03-0.29), which undercuts the mechanism the intervention is named for; quality of life was non-significant (g = 0.20, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.47); and the co-developer of the intervention is an author, which is disclosed. Strong on design, with that mechanism finding and that conflict of interest both material.

(2014) Duration of untreated psychosis as predictor of long-term outcome in schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis. *The British Journal of Psychiatry*, 205 (2): 88-94. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.bp.113.127753 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 33 samples from 54 studies of people with first-episode psychosis, the majority diagnosed with schizophrenia (60-100% of each sample) and at least three in four with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder; mean age at onset 24.4 years (range 12.2-31.5), mean 50.5% male (range 29.8-77.3), mean follow-up 8.1 years (range 2-28); sample sizes at end of follow-up 23 to 776
sources.perspective: psychiatric epidemiology / random-effects meta-analysis of observational first-episode cohorts, with meta-regression
sources.use: Bounds the treatment-delay claim rather than supporting it: every significant correlation is small and three of nine outcomes are null, which is the honest reading the authors themselves give, from a team outside the KCL group.
sources.title: Duration of untreated psychosis as predictor of long-term outcome in schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-structured systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis across seven databases, including non-English publications professionally translated, with stricter diagnostic inclusion than previous meta-analyses, heterogeneity quantified per outcome category, meta-regression on six study-level covariates, and a sensitivity analysis restricted to unadjusted correlations. It can establish that duration of untreated psychosis is associated with worse long-term symptomatic, remission, social-functioning and global outcome, and - just as usefully - that it is **not** significantly associated with employment, quality of life or hospital treatment. It cannot establish that treatment delay causes the worse outcome: every included study is observational, the majority of pooled correlations are unadjusted for confounders, and the authors say the correlation is 'small but mostly consistent'. Moderate rather than strong: only 7 to 19 samples per outcome category, moderate to high heterogeneity in six of nine categories, withdrawal of 4-71% with five samples losing over half their participants, no included study used any statistical method to account for attrition, and the authors had to convert the original effect-size measures into correlations.

sources.population: 53 randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trials of community-oriented family-based psychosocial intervention for people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder; largest single analysis n = 2981 across 32 RCTs
sources.perspective: psychiatry and psychosocial intervention research / Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.use: The plan's strongest single component figure at NNT 7 for relapse, with two fit questions to answer openly, since the population is established schizophrenia and the mechanism is family expressed emotion that a student living away may not have in the room.
sources.title: Family intervention for schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 53 RCTs with a very large pooled sample, giving relative risks with 95% confidence intervals and numbers needed to treat, and reporting a substantial reduction in relapse (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.6, NNT 7) alongside improved medication adherence and reduced expressed emotion. It can establish that family intervention is an evidence-based component of a psychosis treatment plan, and it supplies the NNT a plan can be justified with. It CANNOT be read at face value: the authors state the treatment effects 'may be overestimated due to the poor methodological quality' of the trials, the hospital-admission result crosses 1 (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0), and they note small negative studies may have been missed by the search. It is also NOT first-episode-specific — the population is schizophrenia and schizophrenia-like conditions broadly — and it is a 2010 review, so fifteen years out of date. Moderate rather than strong on the authors' own quality caveat and on fit.

sources.population: 55 studies from 23 countries, majority conducted in North America and Europe; children and adolescents aged 4 to 18, mostly community- or school-based samples
sources.perspective: public health and social epidemiology / systematic review
sources.use: No home as evidence, because the outcome is general psychopathology and psychotic experience is never disaggregated, so it strengthens the stress-vulnerability framing and a two-to-three times figure taken from it would be substitution.
sources.title: Socioeconomic inequalities and mental health problems in children and adolescents: A systematic review.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review that can establish a consistent inverse gradient between socioeconomic status and mental health problems in children and adolescents — 52 of 55 included studies found it, disadvantaged young people being two to three times more likely to develop mental health problems — and can establish that persistent low SES and declining SES are both worse than transient disadvantage, which is a dose and duration finding the corpus otherwise lacks. It CANNOT establish anything about psychosis: the outcome throughout is 'mental health problems', measured by general psychopathology screens, and the review does not disaggregate psychotic experiences. The author lists publication bias and the diversity of SES and outcome measures as limitations, and states that excluding longitudinal studies of over-18s 'restricted the study's ability to observe causal associations over the life course'. Tier is moderate on quality; its FIT for a psychosis essay is POOR.

sources.dataset: Meaning Exploration & Language Behind Anomalous Experiences study (NHS REC reference 22/NW/0375; IRAS 317572)
sources.use: The only source doing Verstehen with real first-episode participants, and it earns its place because the being-in-a-simulation subtheme is never attributed to technology, making it as much a caution against the technology reading as a support for it.
sources.title: Delusion as embodied emotion: a qualitatively driven, multimethod study of first-episode psychosis in the UK
sources.strength_why: A sound primary qualitative study, peer reviewed in The Lancet Psychiatry, open access under CC BY, reported against the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards for Qualitative Research, with the design and protocol developed with a group of people with lived experience, a prior systematic search of the qualitative literature reported in Research in Context, and three analytical standpoints held apart before integration. It answers a question no quantitative design in this corpus asks: what the emergence of a delusion is like from inside, and where its thematic content comes from in the person's own life narrative. It cannot establish prevalence, cause or sequence in any population - the authors state plainly that the study 'does not enable universal generalisations beyond the context and conditions of this study' - and it cannot speak for people who cannot sustain long verbal interviews. Moderate rather than strong because it is a ten-person idiographic study with limitations the authors name themselves: a high proportion of White participants, mostly female, selected for a degree of articulacy.

sources.harvard: Rivera, L. A., Costa-Dookhan, K. A., Raj, V., Dissanayake, J., Siddiqui, I., Hahn, M., Rotenberg, M., Maslej, M. & Foussias, G. (2026) Machine learning methods and schizophrenia spectrum disorders: a scoping review. *BMJ Open*, 16 (9): e112849. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-112849 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 88 peer-reviewed primary studies applying machine learning to outcomes in schizophrenia spectrum disorders; per-study sample sizes ranged from 18 to 24,614 participants; countries of recruitment not reported by the review
sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry and health informatics / PRISMA-ScR scoping review with APPRAISE-AI quality appraisal of every included study
sources.use: The most compact statement of how much weight machine-learning prediction in psychosis can bear, at 47.4 out of 100 on APPRAISE-AI with 20 of 88 studies longitudinal, and its median quality score is arithmetically impossible so must not be quoted.
sources.title: Machine learning methods and schizophrenia spectrum disorders: a scoping review.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-ScR scoping review with a librarian-designed search, dual independent screening and extraction with third-reviewer adjudication and 5% calibration, mapping 88 machine-learning studies in schizophrenia spectrum disorders across five outcome domains, and appraising every one of them with APPRAISE-AI, an instrument built for AI studies supporting clinical decisions. Its most useful finding is about the literature rather than from it: a mean quality score of 47.4 out of 100, with the two weakest domains being robustness of results (mean 9.1/20) and methodological conduct (mean 6.2/20), and most studies either not addressing generalisability at all or naming it only as a limitation. It cannot establish how well any of these models perform: a scoping review by design does not pool, the authors say performance was reported too heterogeneously to synthesise, and the figures they quote are illustrative single studies. Rated moderate rather than strong: the design precludes effect estimates, inclusion was English-language and peer-reviewed only with no grey literature, 70.5% of included studies were cross-sectional, and the paper contains two internal inconsistencies recorded in the reader's note below.

sources.population: 295 patients with an ICD-10 clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia, aged 18-80, able to take part in a productive interview, recruited at Vilnius Mental Health Center, Lithuania
sources.perspective: cultural psychiatry / cross-sectional logistic regression of delusional content on socio-demographic predictors
sources.use: The only study treating delusional content as a dependent variable with odds ratios, and it cuts against the intuitive reading, since religiosity washed out while marital status and education predicted content in a model explaining twelve per cent of variance.
sources.title: Are religious delusions related to religiosity in schizophrenia?
sources.strength_why: The only study found that regresses delusional CONTENT on named predictors and reports odds ratios with confidence intervals, which is the form of evidence a pathoplasticity claim needs and which the rest of the content literature does not supply. It CAN establish, in 295 Lithuanian inpatients assessed with a named content instrument, that religious delusional content was independently predicted by being divorced or separated rather than married (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1-3.5, P=0.019) and by having some postsecondary education (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.4-3.9, P=0.002), while personal religiosity was NOT an independent predictor (adjusted OR 1.7, 95% CI 0.8-3.8) — so the obvious candidate for what shapes religious content does not survive adjustment, and social position does. It also documents that content is gender-patterned: women most often believed they were saints, men that they were God. It CANNOT establish direction, which the authors state plainly, nor much explanatory power: the model's Nagelkerke R-squared is 0.12, so 88% of the variation in whether someone had religious delusions is unaccounted for. Diagnoses were clinical rather than research-interview confirmed, by the authors' own admission. Moderate: full text read, a validated structured instrument, effect sizes with intervals and a genuinely counter-intuitive adjusted result, limited by a cross-sectional single-centre design, unverified diagnoses, a printed confidence interval that cannot be right (see Reader's note) and low model fit.

sources.title: Probability of Transition to Psychosis in Individuals at Clinical High Risk: An Updated Meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA- and MOOSE-compliant meta-analysis of 130 longitudinal studies and 9222 individuals, with independent data extraction, digitisation of published Kaplan-Meier curves to recover survival data, heterogeneity analysis, study-quality assessment and meta-regression. It can establish, with unusual precision for this literature, what proportion of people meeting clinical high-risk criteria go on to develop psychosis and over what period. It cannot establish what predicts transition in an individual, and it inherits the selection bias of the help-seeking samples that clinical high-risk services recruit, so the rates do not transfer to the general population.

(2020) Fostering coping as a mechanism of symptom change in cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis. *Schizophrenia Research*, 215: 416-423. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2019.07.047 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / secondary multilevel mediation analysis of weekly repeated measures within a therapy trial
sources.dataset: a previously published CBTp trial (parent trial not identified in the abstract)
sources.use: The one coping source that tests temporal precedence both ways and finds it, so coping can enter a formulation as a modifiable maintaining factor, in the improvement direction inside therapy, which is not the exacerbation claim it is wanted for.
sources.title: Fostering coping as a mechanism of symptom change in cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis
sources.strength_why: The only source found so far that tests the direction of the coping-symptom relationship rather than assuming it: weekly self-assessments across up to 45 sessions, analysed by multilevel models, with a reverse model fitted as well, which is the right design for a mechanism question and is why it outranks Strous (2005) and MacAulay & Cohen (2013) for this claim despite being smaller. It establishes temporal precedence in an uncontrolled, within-person, treatment-improvement direction: improvement in coping preceded improvement in suspiciousness, negative symptoms and depression. It cannot establish causation or generalise to exacerbation, because it is a secondary analysis of a single uncontrolled therapy sample of 57 people, all measures are self-report, and the mediator and outcome share method and informant. Indicative on sample size, secondary-analysis status and abstract-only access; the design is the reason it is usable at all.

sources.use: The best stress-vulnerability fit on disk for addiction mechanisms, filed with the warning that every mechanism in it runs through drug self-administration, so the behavioural-addiction bridge heavy AI use would need is not built here.
sources.title: Chronic stress, drug use, and vulnerability to addiction.
sources.strength_why: A single-author narrative review that can establish the shape of the stress-addiction vulnerability account — that chronic stress, child maltreatment and accumulated adversity alter CRF/HPA, autonomic and central noradrenergic systems, and that these alterations act on corticostriatal-limbic motivational and learning systems — and can identify where the primary evidence sits. It cannot establish any specific causal pathway, has no search strategy, and is eighteen years old. Used as FOUNDATIONAL framing for a stress-vulnerability model, not as a current statement of the addiction neuroscience literature. Tier is indicative: authoritative review, no primary data, substantially dated.

sources.title: Psychopathology of schizophrenia in Ljubljana (Slovenia) from 1881 to 2000: changes in the content of delusions in schizophrenia patients related to various sociopolitical, technical and scientific changes
sources.strength_why: A retrospective case-note study of 120 randomly selected first-admission records spanning 120 years, which can show that the thematic content of delusions shifted alongside the arrival of radio and television and alongside political change in Slovenia. It cannot establish that the technology caused the shift, nor that the comparison is like for like, because diagnostic practice, recording conventions and the hospital's catchment all changed across the same period and roughly 20 records represent each 20-year span. Indicative rather than moderate because of the small per-period cell sizes and because the appraisal rests on the abstract alone.

sources.title: Polygenic Risk Scores and Twin Concordance for Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder.
sources.strength_why: A twin study that brings two independent methods to bear on the same question — classical twin modelling and molecular polygenic risk scores — in a national twin registry, which is why it can speak to heritability and to whether the molecular and twin estimates agree. It can establish a twin heritability estimate for psychosis of 0.73 and show that polygenic risk predicted co-twin concordance. It cannot support a precise heritability figure: the genotyped sample is small at 292 twins and the 95% confidence interval on the headline estimate runs from 0.30 to 1.00, which is almost the whole admissible range.

sources.population: 490 community-recruited participants (mean age 23.8, SD 5; 80% female, 73% White) at three sites in Glasgow, London and Pavia, pre-screened in two stages with the PQ-16 as the initial screen, then given the full CAARMS/2006 interview
sources.perspective: preventive psychiatry and psychometrics / instrument abbreviation by LASSO-regularised logistic regression in a nested cross-validation framework, with Monte Carlo simulation of prognostic accuracy
sources.use: Says what a clinical determination actually consists of, hours of trained interviewing, and its abstract's unqualified 100% specificity turns out to be a property of the scoring rule rather than measured performance, which e1-assess can use directly.
sources.title: The Mini-CAARMS: Development and Validation of a Short Version of the Comprehensive Assessment of AT Risk Mental States to Facilitate Preventive Psychiatry.
sources.strength_why: A validation study on 490 community participants across three independent UK and Italian sites, abbreviating the 60-item CAARMS/2006 positive-symptom domain to 23 items using LASSO within nested cross-validation, with Cohen's kappa, Harrell's C, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and a Monte Carlo simulation of two-year prognostic accuracy. It is the best source now in the corpus for what a clinician-administered psychosis-risk interview actually CONSISTS of: 60 questions in four aggregate scales, each item rated for severity, frequency, pattern, distress and onset/offset, requiring extensive clinician training and often two hours to administer. Its agreement findings are internal rather than external: the short form is derived from and tested against the same 490 interviews, so kappa 0.90 measures self-consistency with the parent instrument, not accuracy against clinical outcome. The reported specificity of 100% and PPV of 100% are artefacts of the scoring rule, which the authors state plainly in the body and the abstract does not. Prognostic accuracy is simulated, not observed: the authors state they have no follow-up data for this cohort. Rated moderate on that combination of a real multi-site sample and a derivation design that cannot establish prediction.

sources.population: 126 Austrian and 108 Pakistani inpatients and outpatients diagnosed with schizophrenia under DSM-III-R (295)
sources.perspective: cultural psychiatry / cross-cultural comparison of coded delusional content
sources.use: The only study treating who the persecutor is as a separately codeable variable, which is exactly the slot a chatbot occupies, so its full text is the highest-value retrieval left, since Austria against Pakistan is a grouping and not a mechanism.
sources.title: Comparison of delusions among schizophrenics in Austria and in Pakistan
sources.strength_why: The answer to the question of whether anyone has coded delusional content against a predictor rather than against the calendar: 234 patients in two countries, delusional contents classified using the scheme of Huber and Gross, with culture as the comparison. It CAN establish that content differs systematically by culture — significantly higher frequencies of delusions of grandeur, guilt and religious delusions in the Austrian sample — and, crucially for a pathoplasticity argument, that the differences extend to the KIND of persecution and the TYPE OF PERSECUTOR, which were registered as separate variables. That is the only study found anywhere that treats the identity of the persecutor as a codeable, comparable variable, which is the exact slot a chatbot would occupy. It CANNOT establish that any particular agent, technology or stressor produces a particular content: culture here is a two-level grouping variable standing in for everything that differs between Vienna and Lahore, with no mechanism tested and no adjustment reported in the abstract. Nor can it speak to technology at all, in 1999. Moderate: a purpose-designed two-country comparison on a validated content classification with an adequate clinical sample, limited by a crude exposure variable, no reported confounding control, a 1999 diagnostic framework (DSM-III-R), and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

sources.authors: Stompe, T., Ortwein-Swoboda, G., Ritter, K. & Schanda, H.
team: University Hospital for Psychiatry Vienna (Stompe, Ortwein-Swoboda, Ritter, Schanda)
affiliations: University Hospital for Psychiatry Vienna, Austria
sources.harvard: Stompe, T., Ortwein-Swoboda, G., Ritter, K. & Schanda, H. (2003) Old wine in new bottles? Stability and plasticity of the contents of schizophrenic delusions. *Psychopathology*, 36 (1): 6-12. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1159/000069658 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no recruited participants; a synthesis of case reports from the preceding 20 years, long-term thematic comparisons and comparative transcultural studies of delusional content
sources.perspective: cultural psychiatry and psychopathology / narrative synthesis against a stage model of delusion formation
sources.use: The source that most changes what Essay 2 can claim, answering Bokhari's open question with vocabulary rather than form and making persecution the most invariant theme, so the argument has to go through it rather than around it.
sources.title: Old wine in new bottles? Stability and plasticity of the contents of schizophrenic delusions
sources.strength_why: A narrative review that takes on, by name and twenty-three years early, the exact question Essay 2 inherits from Bokhari et al. (2026): whether contemporary technologies supply new delusional content or only new vocabulary. Its answer is the second, and it is the most directly disconfirming source in the corpus for the strong reading of pathoplasticity. It CAN establish that the question has a prior literature with a reasoned answer, and it supplies the conceptual apparatus for that answer — Klosterkotter's three-stage model of delusion formation, in which the 'new' technological material appears only at the third stage, concretisation, over a small set of basic themes (persecution, grandiosity, guilt, religion, hypochondria, jealousy, love) of 'extraordinary anthropological importance'. It also states that persecution and grandiosity showed NO variability over time or between cultures. It CANNOT establish any of this empirically on its own account: it is a narrative synthesis with no stated search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no quality appraisal and no new data, and it reasons from case reports plus the authors' own transcultural work, so its conclusion is an argument rather than a result. Indicative: conceptually load-bearing, methodologically a review article from one group reconciling a literature that includes its own prior studies.

(2006) The pathoplastic effect of culture on psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia. *World Cultural Psychiatry Research Review*, 1 (3/4): 157-163. Available from: https://www.worldculturalpsychiatry.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/10-Pathoplastic-V01N3.pdf (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: the same 1080 consecutively admitted inpatients with schizophrenia as the companion ISPS paper, across Austria, Poland, Lithuania, Georgia, Pakistan, Nigeria and Ghana
sources.perspective: cultural psychiatry / canonical discriminant analysis estimating the culture-attributable share of symptom-content variance
sources.dataset: International Study on Psychotic Symptoms (ISPS), Vienna Research Group in Cultural Psychiatry — the SAME 1080 patients as stompe-2007-paranoid-hallucinatory-isps
sources.use: Puts a number on pathoplasticity, culture accounting for 15 to 30 per cent so that 70 to 85 per cent does not, and carries the authors' own warning that the term is more or less metaphoric, which the thesis had better meet early.
sources.title: The pathoplastic effect of culture on psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: The only study found that puts a NUMBER on pathoplasticity — the share of variance in delusional content, hallucination modality and first-rank symptoms attributable to culture of origin, across 1080 patients in seven countries by canonical discriminant analysis — and the design would support a moderate rating. Its reporting does not. The paper states its one headline figure in THREE mutually inconsistent forms: the abstract says 'rates between 15% and 40%', the results say 'the average correct assignment of psychotic phenomena to countries of origin is between 16 and 40%', and the discussion says 'Between 15% and 30% of the frequencies of contents of delusions, modalities of hallucinations and first rank symptoms may be caused by differences in the cultures of origin'. No single defensible value can be quoted from it. What it CAN carry, robustly, is the complement and the floor: between 70% and 85% of the variance in psychotic symptom prevalence does NOT depend on culture of origin, and chance classification across seven countries is 14.3%, which the authors call a 'gray zone' their estimate sits only a little above. It also records that the term pathoplasticity itself 'has a more or less metaphoric character'. It CANNOT support any causal or mechanistic claim, and it is the same 1080 patients as its companion paper, so the two do not corroborate each other. Indicative: a strong design whose only quantitative claim is reported three ways, in a journal with no DOI.

sources.population: 1080 consecutively admitted inpatients with a clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia, aged 18-60, across seven countries: Austria 350, Poland 80, Lithuania 73, Georgia 74, Pakistan 103, Nigeria 324, Ghana 76. Exclusions: mental disabilities, organic brain disorders, affective and substance-induced disorders
sources.perspective: cultural psychiatry / principal component analysis of coded delusional and hallucinatory content in a seven-country inpatient series
sources.dataset: International Study on Psychotic Symptoms (ISPS), Vienna Research Group in Cultural Psychiatry, founded 1994
sources.use: Settles the negative precisely: the most developed content instrument codes ten themes with none technological and narrates persecutor identity as free text, so a machine persecutor could only ever have been recorded under persecution.
sources.title: Paranoid-hallucinatory syndromes in schizophrenia: results of the International Study on Psychotic Symptoms
sources.strength_why: This is the source that answers the project's decisive question, and it answers it by enumerating an instrument rather than by arguing. It CAN establish, because it prints the taxonomy in full, that the FPS — the instrument behind the largest cross-cultural study of delusional content located anywhere, 1080 consecutively admitted inpatients in seven countries — codes delusional content as exactly TEN binary themes: persecution, poisoning, grandeur, religion, hypochondria, guilt, apocalypse, erotomania, jealousy, descent. Not one is technological, and there is no persecutor-identity category at any level: identity is captured only in a free 'descriptive part' alongside the binary codes. It can also establish that six of seven principal-component syndromes derived from those themes were unequally distributed across the seven sites, delusional jealousy excepted. It CANNOT bear weight on the factor structure itself: the PCA is exploratory with seven factors explaining 11.4% down to 6.5% of variance each, no confirmatory replication, and the paper's own narrative description of factors 4 and 5 contradicts the names it then assigns them. Nor can it speak to technology, in 2007. Moderate: a large, consecutive, multi-site sample with SCID-derived consensus diagnoses and a fully documented instrument, read in full, limited by exploratory factor analysis, several printed inconsistencies, and publication in a small society journal whose peer-review process is evidenced only by printed received and accepted dates.

sources.harvard: Strous, R. D., Ratner, Y., Gibel, A., Ponizovsky, A. & Ritsner, M. (2005) Longitudinal assessment of coping abilities at exacerbation and stabilization in schizophrenia. *Comprehensive Psychiatry*, 46 (3): 167-175. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.comppsych.2004.07.035 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: patients with schizophrenia assessed at exacerbation (n=237) and again at stabilization (n=148) over a 16-month follow-up; hospital services in Israel
sources.perspective: psychiatry / prospective observational cohort with repeated measures and multiple regression
sources.use: No home for the exacerbation claim, since every regression runs coping as the outcome and so reverses the paper's own framing; its narrower uses are that coping is state-dependent and that it is the corpus's only coping source recruited outside Western Europe and the US.
sources.title: Longitudinal assessment of coping abilities at exacerbation and stabilization in schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: A genuinely longitudinal clinical cohort - 237 patients assessed in an acute exacerbation and 148 of them again at stabilization across 16 months - with a validated coping instrument and a wide battery of clinical and psychosocial measures, which is a stronger design than anything else currently available to this project on coping in psychosis. What it establishes is that emotion-oriented coping is used more during exacerbation than during stabilization, and that emotional distress, self-efficacy and social support predict coping style at both phases. What it cannot establish is the direction the argument needs: coping is the DEPENDENT variable in every regression reported, symptom severity is a predictor of it, and symptom severity accounts for only 3.5% of the variance in emotion-oriented coping and 5.5-9% in task-oriented coping. Moderate on design; attrition from 237 to 148 is 37.6% and unexplained in the abstract, and the record is abstract-only.

sources.harvard: Suhail, K. & Cochrane, R. (2002) Effect of culture and environment on the phenomenology of delusions and hallucinations. *International Journal of Social Psychiatry*, 48 (2): 126-138. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1177/002076402128783181 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 201 patients with schizophrenia in three groups: Pakistanis living in Britain (n=53) at All Saints Hospital, Birmingham; Pakistanis in Pakistan (n=98) at two psychiatric units in Lahore; and British White patients (n=50) in Birmingham
sources.perspective: social and cross-cultural psychiatry / three-group comparison of delusional and hallucinatory content coded from case records
sources.use: Ranks first on the content question because its design separates immediate environment from inherited culture, which is the form the pathoplasticity claim actually takes, and it is the one content-coding team with no Stompe on it.
sources.title: Effect of culture and environment on the phenomenology of delusions and hallucinations
sources.strength_why: The best-designed study found on whether delusional content tracks a predictor, because its three-group design does what a simple two-country comparison cannot: by holding ethnicity constant across two environments (Pakistanis in Birmingham versus Pakistanis in Lahore) and environment constant across two ethnicities (Pakistanis versus British White in Birmingham), it separates culture of origin from immediate environment. It CAN establish that content differed more between the two Pakistani groups than between the two Birmingham groups, which the authors read as a stronger influence of the immediate environment than of inherited culture — the most directly pathoplasticity-relevant empirical result located anywhere, and from a team independent of the Vienna group that produced everything else on this question. It also names a content-coding instrument: all references to delusions and hallucinations were coded with the classification scheme of the Present State Examination (Wing et al., 1974). It CANNOT establish any mechanism, and its ascertainment is its weakest point: content was taken from medical records and key-worker reports rather than from direct interview, so what is compared is partly what clinicians in two health systems chose to write down. Moderate: a genuinely informative design on a named coding scheme with an adequate sample, limited by retrospective record-based ascertainment, cross-sectional timing, group sizes of 50-98, and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

Available from: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10597-026-01732-4 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: adults with serious mental illness, including schizophrenia spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder, across three supportive housing facilities in New York City, United States; number of participants not reported in the abstract
sources.perspective: community mental health and peer-informed digital health / secondary qualitative analysis of focus groups
sources.use: The only source where people with serious mental illness discuss AI in their own voice, worth more than its tier suggests, but its population is not psychosis specifically and it is a secondary analysis, so both must be said until the full text is read.
sources.title: Perspectives of People with Serious Mental Illness on Artificial Intelligence-Based Companions: \"If no one told you I love you today, you have someone that cares for you.\
sources.strength_why: Peer reviewed in Community Mental Health Journal, and as far as any search has found it is the only study anywhere that asks people with psychotic disorders directly what they think about AI companions - which is why it is worth having on the record at all. It can indicate what concerns and conditions of trust this population articulates: strong concerns about data privacy and misuse, recognition of potential support for reminders, mental health and daily functioning, greater trust where tools were personalised, human-centred and co-developed, and residual worry about loss of critical thinking and overreliance. It cannot establish how common any of those views are, nor separate the views of people with schizophrenia spectrum disorder from those with bipolar disorder or major depression, because the abstract reports no participant count and no diagnostic breakdown. Indicative rather than moderate for two reasons stated in the abstract itself: it is a **secondary analysis** of three focus groups collected for another purpose, and the full text could not be reached to appraise the sampling, coding or reflexivity.

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / expert narrative overview and implementation argument
sources.use: No home in a first-episode AI plan, and placing it there because the library holds it is the exact failure to avoid; its narrow honest use is the claim that antipsychotics do not treat cognition, itself cited onward to Keefe.
sources.title: Cognitive Remediation Is an Evidence-Based Psychological Therapy: Isn't It Time It Was Treated Like One?
sources.strength_why: An advocacy-framed expert overview, current at 2025, that can establish that cognitive remediation is treated in the field as an evidence-based intervention, that it uses therapeutic formulation in the way other psychological therapies do, and that it is nonetheless inconsistently included in clinical guidelines. It cannot carry an effect size or a recovery claim of its own, because the authors state plainly that they 'have not systematically reviewed the literature but have used expert knowledge and reviews by others'. The authors are among the field's principal proponents, which is relevant to how its conclusions are read. Tier is indicative: a non-systematic review with a stated position.

(2012) Five-year clinical course and outcome of schizophrenia in Ethiopia. *Schizophrenia Research*, 136 (1-3): 137-142. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2011.10.021 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 321 people with schizophrenia identified by screening 68 378 adults aged 15-49 in rural Ethiopia (Butajira); 74.9% had chronic illness at entry and 89.6% were treatment naive
sources.perspective: social psychiatry and global mental health / population-based prospective cohort with 5-year follow-up
sources.dataset: Butajira cohort, rural Ethiopia
sources.use: Disconfirms the comfortable belief that schizophrenia runs a milder course in low-income settings, which makes the corpus's WEIRD base a real limitation rather than a ritual one, though it is neither first-episode nor treated.
sources.title: Five-year clinical course and outcome of schizophrenia in Ethiopia.
sources.strength_why: A population-based prospective cohort with five-year follow-up, built by screening 68 378 adults rather than by sampling clinic attenders, in a setting where 89.6% of cases were treatment naive at entry — a design that is now almost impossible to repeat and that directly tests the long-standing claim of better schizophrenia outcomes in low-income countries. It can establish that the WHO 'better outcome in developing countries' finding does not hold here: 45% were continuously symptomatic, 30.3% had a continuous psychotic episode and only about 20% had continuous remission, and it can establish that being on antipsychotic treatment for at least half the follow-up predicted longer remission (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.12-4.62). It CANNOT establish that treatment caused the better outcome: the treatment exposure is observational, so reverse causation and confounding by severity are open, and the cohort was largely chronic at entry so it is not a first-episode study. Moderate: strong design for its question, non-first-episode population, observational treatment comparison.

Available from: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11469-017-9825-0 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / treatment-programme design paper
sources.use: Useful only as a structural template for what a plan touching everything looks like, since its population is adolescents with gaming disorder, so borrowing its architecture is an argument the essay makes rather than a finding it reports.
sources.title: The treatment of Internet Gaming Disorder: a brief overview of the PIPATIC program.
sources.strength_why: A programme-description paper that can establish what a manualised multi-module adolescent intervention looks like in practice — six modules over six months and twenty-two 45-minute weekly sessions for both individual and family work, designed against CONSORT reporting standards — and is therefore usable as a TEMPLATE for the architecture of a treatment plan. It cannot establish that the programme works: the authors' own word for their outcome data is 'preliminary', and no controlled comparison is reported in this paper. Its population is adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder, not psychosis, so the FIT is structural rather than evidential. Tier is indicative: a design paper with preliminary, uncontrolled outcome data.

sources.population: up to 76,755 individuals with schizophrenia and 243,649 control individuals, two-stage genome-wide association study
sources.perspective: statistical genetics / genome-wide association study with fine-mapping and functional genomics
sources.dataset: Psychiatric Genomics Consortium schizophrenia wave 3 (PGC3-SCZ)
sources.use: Stops the genetic strand sliding into determinism by making it polygenic, and joins two strands of e1-predispose into one argument rather than two lists; reaches e1-what because polygenicity overlapping neurodevelopmental disorders bears on what psychosis is — but not via its heritability clause, which is a secondary citation.
sources.title: Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A two-stage genome-wide association study of up to 76,755 cases and 243,649 controls reporting 287 distinct genome-wide significant loci, with fine-mapping and functional genomic follow-up prioritising 120 genes, published in Nature. It can establish that schizophrenia liability is highly polygenic, that the associated variation is concentrated in genes expressed in central-nervous-system neurons rather than other tissues, and that common and rare variant signals converge. It cannot establish individual-level risk prediction, cannot identify a cause in any one person, and because the heritability figure of 60-80% that opens the paper is cited from prior twin work rather than estimated here, that figure is a secondary citation if used.

sources.harvard: Varese, F., Smeets, F., Drukker, M., Lieverse, R., Lataster, T., Viechtbauer, W., Read, J., van Os, J. & Bentall, R. P. (2012) Childhood adversities increase the risk of psychosis: a meta-analysis of patient-control, prospective- and cross-sectional cohort studies. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 38 (4): 661-671. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbs050 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 41 studies: 18 case-control (2048 psychotic patients, 1856 non-psychiatric controls), 10 prospective/quasi-prospective (n=41,803), 8 population-based cross-sectional (n=35,546)
sources.perspective: psychology / epidemiology, meta-analysis of observational designs
sources.use: Anchors the childhood-adversity strand because its prospective subgroup answers the objection a marker raises first, that psychotic patients recall their childhoods differently.
sources.title: Childhood adversities increase the risk of psychosis: a meta-analysis of patient-control, prospective- and cross-sectional cohort studies.
sources.strength_why: A meta-analysis pooling three different observational designs, which can establish that the adversity-psychosis association is large, consistent and not an artefact of any single design: the overall OR was 2.78 (95% CI 2.34-3.31) and it held separately in prospective studies (OR 2.75, 95% CI 2.17-3.47). It cannot establish causation, cannot separate the timing or dose of adversity, and the authors state that heterogeneity was substantial for every outcome. The tier is strong because it is a design-triangulated meta-analysis with sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates, not because of its size alone.

sources.harvard: Vassos, E., Pedersen, C. B., Murray, R. M., Collier, D. A. & Lewis, C. M. (2012) Meta-analysis of the association of urbanicity with schizophrenia. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 38 (6): 1118-1123. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbs096 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: studies reporting incidence of schizophrenia or non-affective psychosis by level of urbanicity; number of included studies not stated in the abstract
sources.perspective: genetic epidemiology / meta-analysis with simulated individual data points and logistic regression
sources.use: Earns preference over a bare city-living citation because a graded gradient across urbanicity levels is far harder to explain by social drift, though the point estimate needs its interval from the full text first.
sources.title: Meta-analysis of the association of urbanicity with schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A meta-analysis that reframes the urbanicity-schizophrenia association as a linear dose-response on the log odds rather than a most-urban-versus-most-rural comparison, estimating risk in the most urban environment as 2.37 times that in the most rural. It can establish that the association is graded by degree of urbanicity rather than being a city-versus-country dichotomy, which is what makes it useful for a predisposing-factor argument. It cannot establish causation or distinguish social causation from social drift, and the abstract does not state how many studies were included or give a confidence interval for the headline 2.37 figure, so the precision of that estimate cannot be judged from this record.

sources.perspective: neuroscience / selective narrative review with computational modelling
sources.use: Locates the developmental critical period specifically in adolescent prefrontal maturation, the window e1-predispose is about, and is the current-dated, team-independent companion to Keshavan rather than a repetition of him.
sources.title: Psychosis spectrum illnesses as disorders of prefrontal critical period plasticity.
sources.strength_why: A selective narrative review that can establish the existence and shape of the adolescent-prefrontal-critical-period account of psychosis, and is the most current statement of it in this corpus, but cannot evidence any specific causal claim: the authors themselves write that 'the evidence supporting each of these themes is indirect'. It is useful precisely where it is honest — it states that microcircuit function cannot be assessed directly in humans and that macrocircuit plasticity can only be inferred. The tier is indicative because it is a theory synthesis with no primary data, selective rather than systematic in its search.

sources.population: 28 neuroimaging studies of children and adolescents in neurotypical and clinical populations; 871 participants reported by sex (463 male / 408 female), mean of mean ages 9.43 years, range of mean ages 0.59 to 17.3 years

sources.use: The only human, paediatric, systematically searched evidence that experience changes the developing brain, which is the load-bearing premise of the critical-period argument; none of its studies is on psychosis, so it can carry nothing further.
sources.title: Neuroplasticity in children and adolescents in response to treatment intervention: A systematic review of the literature.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 28 neuroimaging studies that can establish that experience-dependent interventions are associated with measurable neuroplastic change in children and adolescents across both neurotypical and clinical populations, and that the construct of neuroplasticity is operationalised inconsistently across that literature. It cannot establish that any particular intervention works or that neuroplastic change corresponds to clinical improvement: the authors state it 'remains unclear' whether the molecular changes map onto cognition and behaviour, and that methodological limitations constrain clinical utility. None of the 28 studies is on psychosis as far as the review's own description goes, so the fit here is to the critical-period argument rather than to any psychosis claim. Tier is moderate: systematic method, substantial heterogeneity, stated limits.

sources.strength_why: A seven-year follow-up of a randomised trial in remitted first-episode psychosis with 80.5% of the original randomised sample located, reporting that the dose-reduction/discontinuation arm had twice the recovery rate of the maintenance arm (40.4% versus 17.6%, OR 3.49, P = .01), driven by functional rather than symptomatic remission. It is the only source found that disconfirms the straightforward 'stay on medication' reading of the relapse evidence, and it does so in exactly the vignette's population — a first episode, in remission. It CANNOT bear a recommendation: the randomisation governed only the first 18 months and treatment after the 2-year trial was 'at the discretion of the clinician', so the seven-year comparison is observational in all but name; it was an open (unblinded) trial; 111 of 257 eligible patients refused, which is a severe selection problem; n is 103 and the primary outcome was not the original trial's; and the authors say 'additional studies are necessary before these results are incorporated into general practice'. Moderate, and the reason is the 18-month randomisation window, not the finding.

sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 44 RCTs and 5142 participants reporting that psychoeducation reduces non-compliance (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.67, NNT 11), relapse (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.81, NNT 9) and readmission (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89, NNT 5), with better social and global functioning and higher service satisfaction. sources.title: Emotional support or problem-solving? A randomized controlled trial of function-specific AI chatbots for digital stress in college students.
sources.strength_why: A genuine three-arm randomised controlled trial with a waitlist control in the vignette's population — university students, selected for elevated digital stress — which is a design the AI-and-mental-health corpus otherwise does not contain at all, and with Chinese participants, which the corpus badly needs. It can establish that a 14-day self-guided generative-AI chatbot can reduce specific dimensions of digital stress, and that function matters: the emotional-support bot reduced availability stress, approval anxiety, social comparison stress and fear of missing out, while the problem-solving bot was better at reducing online vigilance. It CANNOT bear weight on psychosis: there is no psychosis or psychosis-risk outcome anywhere in it, the sample is 99 across three arms so roughly 33 per cell, the follow-up is 14 days, and 'both interventions significantly alleviated anxiety symptoms, whereas effects on depressive symptoms were not significant' — a split result the essay should report rather than round up. Indicative: strong design, very small, very short, and wrong outcome for the claim it would be asked to support.

sources.strength_why: The paper that introduced the CAARMS, reporting what its own authors twice call a pilot and preliminary evaluation: concurrent, discriminant and predictive validity plus inter-rater reliability, tested in an ultra high risk group, a control group and 150 non-psychotic help-seekers followed for six months. It cannot establish how much higher with any useful precision: the relative risk of 12.44 carries a 95% confidence interval of 1.5 to 103.41, a range spanning nearly two orders of magnitude, and the follow-up was six months. sources.title: Interaction with AI companions and psychological well-being
sources.strength_why: The only source found that separates companionship use of a chatbot from instrumental use in real users and attaches an outcome to the distinction, and it does so with behavioural evidence — 464687 messages from donated chat logs — rather than self-report alone, which is what the rest of this corpus runs on. It CAN establish that among 1131 Character.AI users the association between AI companionship and well-being is conditional: reporting companionship as the primary use was associated with lower well-being (beta -0.48, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.25), more so when interactions were intensive (-0.31, CI -0.56 to -0.06) and highly disclosive (-0.38, CI -0.63 to -0.14), and smaller offline social networks were associated with reporting companionship as the primary use (beta -0.03, CI -0.05 to -0.01). It CANNOT establish direction or drift: the design is cross-sectional, so a small social network preceding companionship use and companionship use shrinking a social network fit the data equally, and nothing in it tracks a person moving from instrumental to companion use over time. Nor can it bear weight on psychosis: there is no psychosis or psychosis-risk measure. Moderate: a large, well-reported study in a strong venue with behavioural triangulation and confidence intervals, limited by a self-selected sample of users of one product, a US-only frame, a cross-sectional design, and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

sources.strength_why: The dedicated first-episode evidence synthesis for acute antipsychotic treatment: 19 RCTs, 12 drugs, 2669 participants, with SMDs and ORs and 95% CIs, searching seven databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov without language restriction. It can establish that haloperidol is a suboptimal first choice in first-episode schizophrenia, that differences between second-generation drugs are small, and — the finding that matters most for a treatment plan — that 'the choice of treatment should be guided primarily by side-effects'. sources.strength_why: A theoretical paper, not an empirical study, and the originating statement of the stress-vulnerability model of schizophrenia: it is cited because it is the source of the concept, which is exactly the use foundational work is for. Its age is not a weakness here - a 1977 paper is the correct citation for a 1977 idea, and citing a 2020s textbook for it instead would be a weaker reference, not a stronger one. What it cannot do is carry any empirical weight: it predates neuroimaging, molecular genetics and every modern incidence study, so any claim about the size or mechanism of a risk factor must be cited to current evidence and never to this. Indicative per the tier definition for foundational theory papers; the rating is of evidential weight, not of importance.

clips.note: MISATTRIBUTION, and this clip opens Essay 1. The sentence [quoted wording withheld] is attributed by Boge to World Health Organization (2019), i.e. ICD-11. clips.use: Worth opening for its introduction rather than its results: those two paragraphs are Essay 1's theoretical chain with citations, so use it as a map to those primaries and never as evidence for any of them.
clips.note: RESOLVED, but the claim has to be REWORDED, and the rewording is not cosmetic. Boge's sentence - that differences in coping ability play a role in symptom EXACERBATION - is not supportable. MacAulay & Cohen (2013) does not study exacerbation at all (cross-sectional, 27 patients, headline null, and Boge's sentence traces to MacAulay's own introduction). Strous et al. (2005) is genuinely longitudinal but runs the arrow the OTHER WAY: every regression has coping as the dependent variable and symptoms as a predictor of it, severity explaining 3.5% to 9% of coping variance, and the authors conclude coping [quoted wording withheld]. Using Strous here would reverse its own causal framing - the same error made three times already in this chain. What IS evidenced is narrower and still enough: Schlier et al. (2020) found that [quoted wording withheld], and fitted the reverse model too - improvement in suspiciousness or positive symptoms did NOT predict later coping improvement, though negative symptoms and depression did. So write coping as a MODIFIABLE MAINTAINING FACTOR whose improvement precedes symptom improvement within therapy, not as a deficit that drives exacerbation in untreated psychosis. Four limits travel with it: 57 German outpatients, one group, both measures self-reported by the same person, and individualised positive symptoms conspicuously absent from what coping improvement preceded. Also note Strous's honest use, which is real: coping is STATE-DEPENDENT, emotion-focused coping rising in acute phases - so a coping assessment taken during an acute presentation is measuring a moving target, which is a point the formulation section can use. INDEPENDENCE: Schlier's senior author is Tania Lincoln, who is also Lincoln & Peters (2019) and Lincoln & Heibach (2017), so four links in what looked like a six-source theoretical chain come from one Hamburg group.

clips.note: MINE, not the paper's. Three things constrain how DICE can be used. One-sided testing presupposes the direction of the effect being tested, and with no comparator the p-values carry no inferential weight - cite the d values descriptively and never say DICE "worked". Regression to the mean and expectancy alone would produce this pattern in 10 people given four sessions and daily prompts. The exacerbation dropout is worth one honest sentence: an intervention that asks someone to attend repeatedly to their delusional thinking is not risk-free.

clips.authors: Hudon, A. & Stip, E.
clips.title: Delusional Experiences Emerging From AI Chatbot Interactions or 'AI Psychosis'
clips.strength_why: A peer-reviewed Viewpoint in JMIR Mental Health that defines AI psychosis as a heuristic framework rather than a diagnostic entity and maps it onto the stress-vulnerability model, the digital therapeutic alliance and theory-of-mind accounts. It can establish how the term is used in the published literature and supply a conceptual vocabulary for a mechanism; it cannot establish that the mechanism operates, how often, or in whom, because it reports no data and the authors state the pathways are heuristic and make no causal claim. Indicative rather than weak because it is peer reviewed, explicitly scoped, and the authors are psychiatrists writing within established psychosis models, but it remains opinion rather than evidence.

unplaced.authors: Ajnakina, O., Stubbs, B., Francis, E., Gaughran, F., David, A. S., Murray, R. M. & Lally, J.
unplaced.title: Employment and relationship outcomes in first-episode psychosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies.
unplaced.strength_why: A systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis restricted to LONGITUDINAL studies, pooling 74 cohorts and 15,272 first-episode cases over a mean 8.3 years of follow-up, with meta-regression of moderators. It can establish the scale of functional loss after a first episode in the only design that can: roughly a third are employed and a fifth in a relationship at the end of follow-up, and the employed proportion falls as follow-up lengthens. It also establishes that the pattern is culturally conditional, with higher employment but lower partnership rates in high-income and European settings than in middle-income and non-European ones. It cannot attribute the loss to the illness: these are proportions in exposed cohorts without matched general-population comparators in the pooled analysis, so it quantifies outcome, not causal effect, and it says nothing about education, which it does not measure. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so heterogeneity, risk of bias and publication-bias tests are unverified, and because pooling 74 cohorts with follow-ups ranging from short to decades-long is heterogeneous by construction.

unplaced.authors: Andreasen, N. C., Carpenter, W. T., Kane, J. M., Lasser, R. A., Marder, S. R. & Weinberger, D. R.
unplaced.title: Remission in schizophrenia: proposed criteria and rationale for consensus
unplaced.strength_why: The paper that established the first consensus-based operational criteria for symptomatic remission in schizophrenia, and the one almost every later cohort cites when it says a participant was 'in remission' - including `notes/okeeffe-2021-meaning-in-life-fep.md`, which applies these criteria at 20-year follow-up. It can establish what the field agreed remission means and why it chose thresholds maintained over time rather than change scores. It cannot establish that the criteria are valid, that they predict anything, or that they capture recovery as opposed to symptom level: the authors themselves call the approach novel and say it 'will require further examination of its validity and utility, as well as future refinement, particularly in relation to psychosocial and cognitive function and dysfunction'. Indicative, which is the right tier for an expert consensus statement used for a concept: it is authoritative about a definition and it is not evidence. Rated from the abstract alone - the full text is paywalled - so the specific item thresholds and the six-month duration requirement are recorded here only where a second source in the corpus states them.

(2005) Remission in schizophrenia: proposed criteria and rationale for consensus. *The American Journal of Psychiatry*, 162 (3): 441-449. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.3.441 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

unplaced.authors: Arnold, C., Villagonzalo, K.-A., Meyer, D., Farhall, J., Foley, F., Kyrios, M. & Thomas, N.
unplaced.title: Predicting engagement with an online psychosocial intervention for psychosis: Exploring individual- and intervention-level predictors
unplaced.strength_why: A prospective study of 98 adults with SCID-confirmed psychosis in which the key predictor, asynchronous email support, was randomised and engagement was measured objectively from website logs rather than self-report, so it can establish that light-touch human support raises use of a self-guided online intervention in this population and that externally controlled motivation moderates that effect. It cannot establish that more use produces better clinical outcomes, because no outcome was measured here and the authors say the dose-response relationship may not be linear; nor can it generalise to routine care, because the sample was research-recruited, internet-confident and screened. Moderate rather than strong: the randomised comparison is sound but the sample is small, the predictor set was analysed observationally, and one table is internally inconsistent (see Limitations).

It moves the trauma argument one step past risk of onset — which Varese et al. unplaced.authors: Cantor-Graae, E. & Selten, J. P.

It CANNOT answer the vignette's actual question: the population is schizophrenia broadly rather than first episode, the evidence runs 'approximately up to two years of follow-up' and no further, the suicide and employment analyses are underpowered and low-certainty, and randomisation, allocation and blinding were 'poorly reported' in many included studies. unplaced.strength_why: The only empirical test of case formulation in psychosis I could locate, and it is a largely NULL and partly adverse result: across two experiments, formulation 'had little or no impact' on perceived therapeutic relationship, on strength of delusional and self-evaluative beliefs, or on anxiety and depression; therapists' own ratings of the relationship improved while clients' did not, and six clients found formulation at least in part a negative experience. It CANNOT establish that formulation is useless — it is small, uncontrolled, single-site, from one service, over twenty years old and predates the Five Ps version of the framework, and the abstract does not report the sample size. Indicative on design; its FIT to the claim that a formulation-based plan is justified is high precisely because it qualifies it.

It is the best available evidence that a coordinated multimodal service — not any single modality — outperforms ordinary care in early-phase psychosis, and its inclusion criteria define that service as combining psychosocial AND psychopharmacological components delivered by one team, which is the direct evidence that a plan touching several domains beats a referral chain. It CANNOT establish which component does the work: the unit of randomisation is the service, so the meta-analysis is silent on the contribution of medication, family work, vocational support or psychotherapy taken separately. unplaced.strength_why: A PRISMA-ScR scoping review with a registered protocol that maps the whole construct of problematic AI use across 37 empirical studies, and the only source found that answers the measurement question directly. It CAN establish that the construct exists in the literature but is not settled: terminology is inconsistent, definitions are frequently absent altogether in eight of the included studies, AI-specific instruments do exist — the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale, built on the DSM-5-TR Internet Gaming Disorder framework, and the AI Chatbot Dependence Scale — but most measurement borrows scales for social media, smartphones, mobile applications, computers and in one case fast food, which the authors argue 'presuppose rather than test' that problematic AI use has the same structure. It can also establish that the evidence base is 30 quantitative and 7 mixed-method studies, overwhelmingly cross-sectional. It CANNOT establish prevalence, direction or any causal claim, and the authors say so: 'The predominance of cross-sectional studies limits conclusions about the directionality of key associations ... precludes conclusions about whether, for instance, loneliness leads to problematic AI use or whether problematic AI use exacerbates loneliness.' Moderate rather than strong: a transparent, registered scoping review with a careful construct critique, but a scoping review performs no risk-of-bias assessment by design, searched only Web of Science and Scopus, and was restricted to English.

unplaced.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD42020185030) random-effects meta-analysis with no language or time restriction, pooling 37 observational studies (n=7,717) from 25 countries that used one of two validated self-stigma scales, with subgroup and meta-regression analysis of associated factors. It can establish that self-stigma is measurable and substantial across six dimensions in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, that pooled levels did not reduce over the 2007-2020 publication window, and that the correlates are social and iatrogenic (unemployment, low income, singleness, living outside urban areas, high antipsychotic dose, low functioning) rather than illness-severity indices, since psychotic severity, age at onset, illness duration, age, sex and education were NOT associated. It cannot establish direction: every included study is observational and the review reports association, so it cannot say whether stigma follows impaired functioning or helps produce it. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so no risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity statistic or funnel-plot analysis has been verified, and the pooled means are scale scores on a 1-4 range rather than an interpretable clinical threshold.

unplaced.title: Psychological investigation of the structure of paranoia in a non-clinical population
unplaced.strength_why: A large (n=1202) multidimensional questionnaire survey that established the continuum position for paranoia: the count of suspicious thoughts followed a single continuous, near-exponential distribution with no distinct subpopulation, and rarer, odder suspicions sat on top of commoner emotional concerns in a hierarchy. It can establish that paranoid thinking is common and continuously distributed in a non-clinical population and that it is structured rather than random; it cannot establish prevalence in any general population, nor causal direction, because the sample is a self-selected student convenience sample recruited by e-mail and the design is cross-sectional — both of which the authors state. Moderate rather than strong because of the sampling, not the analysis.

unplaced.authors: Gao, Q., Zhu, P. & Hu, H.
unplaced.title: Factors associated with aggressive behavior in patients with schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
unplaced.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD420251147415), PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis searching ten databases, six English and four Chinese (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, CBM), 2014 to October 2024, with Newcastle-Ottawa quality scoring (mostly 7-9 of 9), sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and funnel plots. It can establish the strength of association between a defined set of correlates and aggression in people already diagnosed with schizophrenia, with pooled odds ratios and confidence intervals. It cannot establish causation or anything about the onset of psychosis: the authors state that the included studies were 'primarily case-control and cross-sectional studies, which limit causal inference regarding etiology', and the outcome 'aggressive behavior' had no standardised operational definition across the primary studies. Current, not foundational. Fit caveat, which matters more here than the tier: this is violence risk in established schizophrenia, a different construct and a different population from first-episode or clinical high-risk psychosis, so it cannot carry any predisposing-factor claim in Essay 1.

unplaced.title: Evidence-based interventions for vocational recovery in first-episode psychosis: A meta-analysis of employment and education rates.
unplaced.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered PRISMA meta-analysis of 31 studies (n=8,651) with formal risk-of-bias assessment (RoB2 and ROBINS-E) and GRADE certainty rating, analysing employment, education and combined vocational rates both as pooled proportions and as intervention-versus-control comparisons. It can establish that vocational intervention improves competitive employment after a first episode (overall OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.88-2.94; Individual Placement and Support OR 2.86, 95% CI 1.81-4.54) and - the more useful half for this project - that no intervention showed a consistent advantage for EDUCATION rates, with a confidence interval that includes no effect (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.80-1.76). It cannot establish much about the combined endpoint, which the authors themselves describe as limited in interpretability by substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 69.6%, tau-squared 0.296, p<0.001) and possible publication bias. Rated moderate rather than strong because the full text could not be reached, so the GRADE certainty ratings, the per-outcome risk-of-bias judgements, the countries of included studies and the definitions of 'education' are all unverified, and because an online-first record carries no volume, issue or page numbers.

unplaced.authors: Gupta, T., Deam, M., Headley, E., Seah, T. H. S., Silk, J., Griffith, J. M., Vargas, T., Messineo, S. & Horton, L.
unplaced.title: Trajectories of distressing psychotic-like experience in youth: the interplay of recent negative life events and screen time
unplaced.strength_why: The only source found that puts adversity and digital media in the same prospective model with a psychosis-relevant outcome, which is exactly where the corpus's trauma strand and its technology strand fail to meet. Its strength is not uniform and should not be cited as if it were. The TRAJECTORY findings are moderate and rest on the full cohort: latent growth mixture modelling over five timepoints in 11867 ABCD participants gave an increasing PLE-distress class (n=409), a decreasing class (n=698) and a no-distress class (n=10759), and youth in the increasing class reported more recent negative life events while reporting similar total daily screen time to the decreasing class — so adversity, not screen volume, is what separates the two symptomatic trajectories. The MODERATION findings, which are the ones an essay would actually want, are indicative at best: the weekend screen time x negative life events interaction (B 0.51, SE 0.19, t 2.74, P=.007, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.86) comes from a mixed model with n=103, the weekday equivalent was NOT significant (P=.12), and the texting and social-media results the abstract leads with are labelled exploratory in the body and carry t(90). It CANNOT establish that screen use causes PLE distress, cannot speak to AI or chatbots at all, and its 4-year outcome data were released for only around 40% of the cohort with the increasing-distress trajectory differentially under-represented. Moderate overall, with the carve-out stated.

unplaced.title: Neurobiology of early life adversity: A systematic review of meta-analyses towards an integrative account of its neurobiological trajectories to mental disorders.
unplaced.strength_why: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 27 meta-analyses that can establish convergent neurobiological correlates of adverse childhood experiences across four previously separate literatures — HPA axis, inflammation, neuroimaging and genetics/epigenetics — and can establish that those correlates appear in people with and without a psychiatric diagnosis, which is a real and unusual finding. It cannot establish causation and the authors call for longitudinal work to do so; it is also a review of reviews, so it is three steps from any participant and inherits every constituent meta-analysis's bias. Its outcome is mental disorders in general, NOT psychosis, which limits its fit here. Tier is moderate: rigorous method, stated limitations, but an umbrella design on a non-specific outcome.
