unplaced.authors: Hardy, A., Emsley, R., Freeman, D., Bebbington, P., Garety, P. A., Kuipers, E. E., Dunn, G. & Fowler, D.
unplaced.title: Psychological mechanisms mediating effects between trauma and psychotic symptoms: the role of affect regulation, intrusive trauma memory, beliefs, and depression
unplaced.strength_why: The best source found for the proposition that childhood adversity is associated with the TYPE of psychotic symptom and not only with risk or severity, and it is a clinical sample of 228 people with relapsing psychosis rather than a student or community survey. It CAN establish specificity in this sample: childhood emotional abuse was associated with persecutory and referential delusions while childhood sexual abuse was associated with auditory hallucinations, and the persecutory association was statistically mediated by negative beliefs about other people. It CANNOT establish temporal order or cause, and the authors say so themselves — 'The study was cross-sectional and future work should investigate these processes in prospective or longitudinal studies'; trauma was recalled retrospectively by people who already had psychosis, PTSD symptoms were self-reported rather than interviewed, and the mediation models for hallucinations rest on n = 118 complete cases, not 228. Moderate rather than strong: a well-specified a priori hypothesis set with a counterfactual mediation framework and a representativeness check against trial non-completers, against a cross-sectional design, retrospective recall, and a symptom coding that collapses 0-5 severity scales to present/absent.

unplaced.title: Predicting PANSS symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorders using speech only: an international, multi-centre, retrospective, computational study across multiple languages.
unplaced.strength_why: A medRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Version 1 was posted 28 February 2026 and version 2 on 30 September 2026; the medRxiv API returns `published: NA` for both as of 12 October 2026, so no journal version exists to cite instead. Under this project's appraisal tiers a preprint is not-citable where a peer-reviewed alternative exists, and for the specific question it answers - item-level PANSS prediction from speech alone across ten languages - no peer-reviewed alternative exists at all, which is why it is filed rather than discarded. Judged on publication status, not on method: the method as described is strong for its genre (speaker-disjoint splits, 16 algorithms compared per item, bias checks by age, sex, education and severity, models released), and the authors' own stated limitation is that the dataset is heterogeneous in samples, languages, symptom assessment and speech elicitation. Nothing from it may enter the essays as evidence. It may be mentioned as a preprint, with that word attached, or used to locate the primary site studies it pooled.

unplaced.authors: He, M., Ding, X., Liu, X. & Wang, D.
unplaced.title: Longitudinal bidirectional relationships between problematic smartphone use and psychotic-like experiences among young adults: the mediating role of excessive daytime sleepiness
unplaced.strength_why: The only prospective study found anywhere on a technology the corpus's argument is actually about: smartphone use and psychotic-like experiences, three waves at six-month intervals, 6153 young adults, with within-person modelling that separates change in a person from differences between people. It CAN establish temporal order in this sample, and the order runs the way the argument does not want: after accounting for stable between-person differences the random-intercept model 'provided no evidence for a bidirectional association', and the surviving within-person path was increases in psychotic-like experiences at Time 1 predicting increases in problematic smartphone use at Time 3 through daytime sleepiness at Time 2. It CANNOT establish anything about generative AI, chatbots or conversational agents — the exposure is problematic smartphone use as a global construct — nor about diagnosed psychosis, since the outcome is self-reported psychotic-like experiences in a non-clinical student sample. Moderate rather than strong: a large, genuinely prospective, within-person design with the right comparison of CLPM against RI-CLPM, against entirely self-reported exposure and outcome, an 79.7% female sample, a single-country single-population frame, and a record read from the abstract only, so no effect sizes, intervals or attrition have been checked.

unplaced.title: Association between cannabis use disorder and schizophrenia stronger in young males than in females.
unplaced.strength_why: A nationwide register cohort covering 6,907,859 people and 129,521,260 person-years with 45,327 incident schizophrenia cases, which effectively removes selection and recall bias from exposure and outcome measurement and is large enough to estimate sex- and age-stratified effects and population attributable fractions over fifty years. unplaced.authors: Howes, O. D. & Kapur, S.
unplaced.title: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: version III--the final common pathway
unplaced.strength_why: The field's canonical statement of the current dopamine hypothesis, peer reviewed in Schizophrenia Bulletin, open access, and the paper that explicitly ties dopamine dysfunction to psychotic experience through aberrant salience - the mechanism `notes/bokhari-2026-technology-delusions.md` already leans on without the corpus holding a primary for it. It can establish what the hypothesis now claims, that elevated presynaptic striatal dopamine synthesis capacity is the most widely replicated dopaminergic abnormality in schizophrenia with reported effect sizes of 0.63 to 1.89 across seven of nine studies, that striatal dopamine elevation is absent in mania, depression and non-psychotic psychiatric disorders, and that the authors locate the abnormality with **psychosis** rather than with schizophrenia as a diagnosis. It cannot establish causation, direction or sequence: it is a selective review of cross-sectional case-control PET studies, the measures are indirect indices rather than dopamine levels, and the authors say the hypothesis 'will be revised as more data become available'. Moderate rather than strong because it is a selective narrative synthesis with no stated search strategy or risk-of-bias assessment, and because the imaging evidence it rests on is almost entirely small-sample - see the appraisal against Marek et al. below.

unplaced.authors: iheed / University of Warwick, MSc Neuroscience and Psychology of Mental Health
unplaced.title: M6W4 – Evidence-Based Treatments for Complex Mental Health Conditions
unplaced.strength_why: Course teaching slides, unattributed to a named author, not peer reviewed and not publicly retrievable, so it cannot be cited as evidence for any claim in either essay — citing it would also be citing course notes, which the Module 3 brief explicitly asks students to distinguish from their own ideas and to reference properly. Its value is entirely as a SPECIFICATION of what the marker expects: it fixes the course's own wording of the 5Ps, of holistic formulation and of Verstehen, and it names the psychosis treatment list the assessment assumes. Every substantive point it makes must be re-sourced to a primary or secondary publication before it enters the essay. Tier is not-citable by definition of the venue, not by any defect in the content.

unplaced.authors: Jahshan, C., Rassovsky, Y. & Green, M. F.
unplaced.title: Enhancing neuroplasticity to augment cognitive remediation in schizophrenia.
unplaced.strength_why: A short mini-review, team-independent of the Vinogradov lineage, that can establish that response to cognitive remediation is highly variable, that combining it with exercise or tDCS is a live research strategy, and that the mechanistic rationale runs through BDNF and long-term potentiation. It cannot establish that the combination works: the authors state there are 'insufficient data to determine if this multimodal approach leads to incremental performance gain in patients' and call for larger RCTs. Nine years old and the tDCS literature has grown substantially since, so any claim about the state of that evidence must be dated. Tier is indicative: a mini-review with no primary data and explicitly insufficient evidence on its own question.

unplaced.authors: Jauhar, S., McKenna, P. J., Radua, J., Fung, E., Salvador, R. & Laws, K. R.
unplaced.title: Cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis with examination of potential bias
unplaced.strength_why: A PRISMA systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 52 randomised trials, pre-specified moderator analyses for three Cochrane risk-of-bias domains plus use of a control intervention, and three separate publication-bias tests: it is the primary source for every effect size the 2019 editorial reports, and it is the strongest treatment-efficacy source now in the corpus. It establishes that pooled end-of-treatment effects of CBT on overall, positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia lie in the small range and that masking of outcome assessment significantly moderates them, with positive symptoms falling to non-significance in masked trials. Its own stated limits are real: the low-risk-of-bias subanalyses rest on 8-11 studies because most trials were rated 'unclear' rather than low or high risk, and it did not examine effects on depression, anxiety or distress, so it can say nothing about those. Full appraisal from the full text; strong on design and directly on the claim.

unplaced.strength_why: An editorial 'critical viewpoint', not an independent synthesis: it reports effect sizes drawn from other meta-analyses, one of which is the authors' own (Jauhar et al., 2014), and it has no protocol, no search strategy and no risk-of-bias assessment of its own. It can establish that the pooled effect of CBTp on positive symptoms in meta-analyses published since 2014 lies in the small range, that the effect attenuates under blinding, and that these authors read the evidence as not supporting CBTp for negative symptoms or relapse prevention. It cannot stand as the source of an effect-size figure, because every number in it is secondary; for those, cite Jauhar et al. (2014), British Journal of Psychiatry, 204 (1): 20-29, directly. Indicative rather than moderate because of the publication type and the authors' declared position in the controversy.

unplaced.strength_why: A Cochrane review with a registered protocol, a specialist trials register searched without language or publication-status limits, independent duplicate screening and extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE rating: the strongest design in the corpus for a treatment question. What it establishes is narrow and often misread: it compares CBT against OTHER psychosocial therapies as add-ons, not against standard care alone, and it found no clear difference on relapse, rehospitalisation, mental state, death, social functioning or quality of life. It therefore cannot be cited for the size of CBTp's effect against treatment-as-usual, and the authors themselves rate the evidence as mainly low or very low quality. unplaced.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review (CRD42018086800) screening 56,721 records to 177 included studies, with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression that tests study method as an explanation for the variation it finds. unplaced.authors: Kapur, S.
unplaced.title: Psychosis as a state of aberrant salience: a framework linking biology, phenomenology, and pharmacology in schizophrenia
unplaced.strength_why: The primary source for aberrant salience: the paper that proposed dopamine's role as mediating the salience of events and representations, and that delusions are the person's own cognitive effort to make sense of aberrantly salient experience while hallucinations are the direct experience of aberrant salience in internal representations. It can establish what the framework claims and where it came from, which is what the corpus needs, because the mechanism is currently cited through `notes/bokhari-2026-technology-delusions.md` and restated in `notes/howes-2009-dopamine-hypothesis-iii.md`. It cannot establish anything empirically: it collects no data, tests nothing, and the author describes it as 'a heuristic framework' and discusses its limitations himself. Indicative is the tier for a theory paper used for a concept - it is foundational and it is not evidence, and no amount of citation makes a framework a finding. Rated from the abstract and from Howes and Kapur's (2009) restatement of it; the full text is paywalled.

unplaced.title: Loneliness in psychosis: a meta-analytical review.
unplaced.strength_why: A random-effects meta-analysis of 13 studies and 15 647 participants with study and outcome quality assessed using adapted AHRQ and GRADE tools, finding a moderate association between loneliness and psychotic symptoms (r = .32, 95% CI 0.20-0.44) that did not depend on whether loneliness was measured by a single item or a full scale — a measurement-robustness check that matters, because the single-item objection is the obvious one. It can establish that loneliness and psychotic symptoms covary at a clinically meaningful magnitude, which is what lets social isolation be treated as a target rather than a backdrop. It CANNOT establish direction or cause: the authors say explicitly that 'further studies are needed to determine the causal status of this relationship', the included studies are correlational, and heterogeneity is extreme at I-squared = 97.56%, so the pooled r of .32 summarises a very dispersed set of estimates. The authors rate their own evidence 'moderate quality'.

unplaced.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
unplaced.title: Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management. NICE clinical guideline CG178.
unplaced.strength_why: A national clinical guideline developed through NICE's published process: commissioned systematic reviews, a multidisciplinary committee including service users and carers, consultation, and dated versioning with an audit trail of what changed and when. For the question 'what should a care plan for psychosis contain, and on whose authority', nothing outranks it in a UK context, and it is the document a UK marker will expect a holistic plan to be measured against. It establishes the expected SHAPE of care - oral antipsychotic plus family intervention and individual CBT at first episode, crisis resolution and home treatment as the first-line crisis service, supported employment, physical health monitoring, carer support, peer support and self-management - and it does so at the level of detail a 500-word plan can actually use. It establishes NOTHING about whether any of those interventions works: it is a consensus synthesis, so its recommendations are a committee's judgement on evidence, not evidence, and several load-bearing recommendations are marked [2009], meaning their last evidence review was in 2009. Essay 2 may cite it for what a plan should include and must not cite it for efficacy.

unplaced.strength_why: A national guideline developed through NICE's documented process, with named evidence reviews cited against each recommendation group (reviews A, C, E, F, G, I and P), covering a territory CG178 barely touches: rehabilitation pathways, supported accommodation, structured daily and group activity, supported employment, and team formulation. For the question 'what does rehabilitation actually consist of, and on whose authority', it is the UK authority and the only source in this corpus that addresses housing at all. It establishes the expected CONTENT of a rehabilitation and recovery plan - supported accommodation, daily living skills, structured group social and leisure activity, IPS-model supported employment, recovery colleges, and mindfulness among the additional psychological interventions - at a level a short plan can cite in one go. It establishes NOTHING about efficacy: it is a consensus synthesis, and it is scoped to COMPLEX psychosis, meaning treatment-resistant symptoms with impaired functioning, so it is the wrong citation for a first-episode or recent-onset case without saying so explicitly.

unplaced.authors: O'Keeffe, D., Keogh, B. & Higgins, A.
unplaced.title: Meaning in Life in Long-Term Recovery in First-Episode Psychosis: An Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis
unplaced.strength_why: A sound primary qualitative study: IPA conducted inside an epidemiologically complete FEP incidence cohort, with purposive maximum-variation sampling deliberately balanced across remission status, age at onset and gender, Yardley's four quality criteria applied and documented action by action, three analysis phases, personal and epistemological reflexivity reported, and the authors' own limitations stated at length. It answers what recovery and meaning are like from the service user's own standpoint two decades after a first episode - a question no outcome scale in this corpus asks - and it supplies an operational definition of first-episode psychosis and the remission criteria the cohort used. It cannot establish how common any of these experiences is, nor how meaning is experienced soon after onset, because every account is retrospective by about 21 years and the authors name recall bias themselves. Moderate rather than strong: 16 people, all Caucasian, mostly male, mostly unemployed, with possible recruitment bias towards those already interested in meaning in life, and the sample was not balanced across baseline diagnoses.

unplaced.title: Trajectories of Adolescent Media Use and Their Associations With Psychotic Experiences.
unplaced.strength_why: The only genuinely prospective source in this corpus on digital media use and psychotic experiences: a population birth cohort followed from 5 months to 23 years, with exposure reported at ages 12, 13, 15 and 17 and the outcome measured at 23, so the temporal order is fixed by design rather than by recall, and with adjustment for sociodemographic, genetic, family and childhood covariables measured between 5 months and 12 years. It can establish that adolescent media-use trajectories are at most MODESTLY associated with psychotic experiences in young adulthood, and - more usefully - that part of what looks like an effect is confounding by prior mental health: higher video gaming 'was preceded by higher levels of mental health and interpersonal problems at age 12 years', and adjusting for those 'mitigated the association'. Only ONE association survived adjustment - a curved trajectory of computer use, n=189 - and the authors' own conclusion attributes the findings 'likely' to shared risk factors. Strong on design; the fit to an AI claim is poor and must be stated.

unplaced.title: Immediate and sustained outcomes and moderators associated with metacognitive training for psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

unplaced.title: Duration of untreated psychosis as predictor of long-term outcome in schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis

unplaced.title: Family intervention for schizophrenia.
unplaced.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 53 RCTs with a very large pooled sample, giving relative risks with 95% confidence intervals and numbers needed to treat, and reporting a substantial reduction in relapse (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.6, NNT 7) alongside improved medication adherence and reduced expressed emotion. It can establish that family intervention is an evidence-based component of a psychosis treatment plan, and it supplies the NNT a plan can be justified with. It CANNOT be read at face value: the authors state the treatment effects 'may be overestimated due to the poor methodological quality' of the trials, the hospital-admission result crosses 1 (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0), and they note small negative studies may have been missed by the search. It is also NOT first-episode-specific — the population is schizophrenia and schizophrenia-like conditions broadly — and it is a 2010 review, so fifteen years out of date. Moderate rather than strong on the authors' own quality caveat and on fit.

unplaced.title: Are religious delusions related to religiosity in schizophrenia?
unplaced.strength_why: The only study found that regresses delusional CONTENT on named predictors and reports odds ratios with confidence intervals, which is the form of evidence a pathoplasticity claim needs and which the rest of the content literature does not supply. It CAN establish, in 295 Lithuanian inpatients assessed with a named content instrument, that religious delusional content was independently predicted by being divorced or separated rather than married (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1-3.5, P=0.019) and by having some postsecondary education (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.4-3.9, P=0.002), while personal religiosity was NOT an independent predictor (adjusted OR 1.7, 95% CI 0.8-3.8) — so the obvious candidate for what shapes religious content does not survive adjustment, and social position does. It also documents that content is gender-patterned: women most often believed they were saints, men that they were God. It CANNOT establish direction, which the authors state plainly, nor much explanatory power: the model's Nagelkerke R-squared is 0.12, so 88% of the variation in whether someone had religious delusions is unaccounted for. Diagnoses were clinical rather than research-interview confirmed, by the authors' own admission. Moderate: full text read, a validated structured instrument, effect sizes with intervals and a genuinely counter-intuitive adjusted result, limited by a cross-sectional single-centre design, unverified diagnoses, a printed confidence interval that cannot be right (see Reader's note) and low model fit.

unplaced.strength_why: The answer to the question of whether anyone has coded delusional content against a predictor rather than against the calendar: 234 patients in two countries, delusional contents classified using the scheme of Huber and Gross, with culture as the comparison. It CAN establish that content differs systematically by culture — significantly higher frequencies of delusions of grandeur, guilt and religious delusions in the Austrian sample — and, crucially for a pathoplasticity argument, that the differences extend to the KIND of persecution and the TYPE OF PERSECUTOR, which were registered as separate variables. That is the only study found anywhere that treats the identity of the persecutor as a codeable, comparable variable, which is the exact slot a chatbot would occupy. It CANNOT establish that any particular agent, technology or stressor produces a particular content: culture here is a two-level grouping variable standing in for everything that differs between Vienna and Lahore, with no mechanism tested and no adjustment reported in the abstract. Nor can it speak to technology at all, in 1999. Moderate: a purpose-designed two-country comparison on a validated content classification with an adequate clinical sample, limited by a crude exposure variable, no reported confounding control, a 1999 diagnostic framework (DSM-III-R), and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

unplaced.title: Old wine in new bottles? Stability and plasticity of the contents of schizophrenic delusions
unplaced.strength_why: A narrative review that takes on, by name and twenty-three years early, the exact question Essay 2 inherits from Bokhari et al. (2026): whether contemporary technologies supply new delusional content or only new vocabulary. Its answer is the second, and it is the most directly disconfirming source in the corpus for the strong reading of pathoplasticity. It CAN establish that the question has a prior literature with a reasoned answer, and it supplies the conceptual apparatus for that answer — Klosterkotter's three-stage model of delusion formation, in which the 'new' technological material appears only at the third stage, concretisation, over a small set of basic themes (persecution, grandiosity, guilt, religion, hypochondria, jealousy, love) of 'extraordinary anthropological importance'. It also states that persecution and grandiosity showed NO variability over time or between cultures. It CANNOT establish any of this empirically on its own account: it is a narrative synthesis with no stated search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no quality appraisal and no new data, and it reasons from case reports plus the authors' own transcultural work, so its conclusion is an argument rather than a result. Indicative: conceptually load-bearing, methodologically a review article from one group reconciling a literature that includes its own prior studies.

unplaced.authors: Stompe, T., Karakula, H., Rudalevičiene, P., Okribelashvili, N., Chaudhry, H. R., Idemudia, E. E. & Gscheider, S.
unplaced.title: The pathoplastic effect of culture on psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia
unplaced.strength_why: The only study found that puts a NUMBER on pathoplasticity — the share of variance in delusional content, hallucination modality and first-rank symptoms attributable to culture of origin, across 1080 patients in seven countries by canonical discriminant analysis — and the design would support a moderate rating. Its reporting does not. The paper states its one headline figure in THREE mutually inconsistent forms: the abstract says 'rates between 15% and 40%', the results say 'the average correct assignment of psychotic phenomena to countries of origin is between 16 and 40%', and the discussion says 'Between 15% and 30% of the frequencies of contents of delusions, modalities of hallucinations and first rank symptoms may be caused by differences in the cultures of origin'. No single defensible value can be quoted from it. What it CAN carry, robustly, is the complement and the floor: between 70% and 85% of the variance in psychotic symptom prevalence does NOT depend on culture of origin, and chance classification across seven countries is 14.3%, which the authors call a 'gray zone' their estimate sits only a little above. It also records that the term pathoplasticity itself 'has a more or less metaphoric character'. It CANNOT support any causal or mechanistic claim, and it is the same 1080 patients as its companion paper, so the two do not corroborate each other. Indicative: a strong design whose only quantitative claim is reported three ways, in a journal with no DOI.

unplaced.title: Paranoid-hallucinatory syndromes in schizophrenia: results of the International Study on Psychotic Symptoms
unplaced.strength_why: This is the source that answers the project's decisive question, and it answers it by enumerating an instrument rather than by arguing. It CAN establish, because it prints the taxonomy in full, that the FPS — the instrument behind the largest cross-cultural study of delusional content located anywhere, 1080 consecutively admitted inpatients in seven countries — codes delusional content as exactly TEN binary themes: persecution, poisoning, grandeur, religion, hypochondria, guilt, apocalypse, erotomania, jealousy, descent. Not one is technological, and there is no persecutor-identity category at any level: identity is captured only in a free 'descriptive part' alongside the binary codes. It can also establish that six of seven principal-component syndromes derived from those themes were unequally distributed across the seven sites, delusional jealousy excepted. It CANNOT bear weight on the factor structure itself: the PCA is exploratory with seven factors explaining 11.4% down to 6.5% of variance each, no confirmatory replication, and the paper's own narrative description of factors 4 and 5 contradicts the names it then assigns them. Nor can it speak to technology, in 2007. Moderate: a large, consecutive, multi-site sample with SCID-derived consensus diagnoses and a fully documented instrument, read in full, limited by exploratory factor analysis, several printed inconsistencies, and publication in a small society journal whose peer-review process is evidenced only by printed received and accepted dates.

unplaced.title: Longitudinal assessment of coping abilities at exacerbation and stabilization in schizophrenia
unplaced.strength_why: A genuinely longitudinal clinical cohort - 237 patients assessed in an acute exacerbation and 148 of them again at stabilization across 16 months - with a validated coping instrument and a wide battery of clinical and psychosocial measures, which is a stronger design than anything else currently available to this project on coping in psychosis. What it establishes is that emotion-oriented coping is used more during exacerbation than during stabilization, and that emotional distress, self-efficacy and social support predict coping style at both phases. Moderate on design; attrition from 237 to 148 is 37.6% and unexplained in the abstract, and the record is abstract-only.

unplaced.authors: Suhail, K. & Cochrane, R.
unplaced.title: Effect of culture and environment on the phenomenology of delusions and hallucinations
unplaced.strength_why: The best-designed study found on whether delusional content tracks a predictor, because its three-group design does what a simple two-country comparison cannot: by holding ethnicity constant across two environments (Pakistanis in Birmingham versus Pakistanis in Lahore) and environment constant across two ethnicities (Pakistanis versus British White in Birmingham), it separates culture of origin from immediate environment. It CAN establish that content differed more between the two Pakistani groups than between the two Birmingham groups, which the authors read as a stronger influence of the immediate environment than of inherited culture — the most directly pathoplasticity-relevant empirical result located anywhere, and from a team independent of the Vienna group that produced everything else on this question. It also names a content-coding instrument: all references to delusions and hallucinations were coded with the classification scheme of the Present State Examination (Wing et al., 1974). It CANNOT establish any mechanism, and its ascertainment is its weakest point: content was taken from medical records and key-worker reports rather than from direct interview, so what is compared is partly what clinicians in two health systems chose to write down. Moderate: a genuinely informative design on a named coding scheme with an adequate sample, limited by retrospective record-based ascertainment, cross-sectional timing, group sizes of 50-98, and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

unplaced.strength_why: Peer reviewed in Community Mental Health Journal, and as far as any search has found it is the only study anywhere that asks people with psychotic disorders directly what they think about AI companions - which is why it is worth having on the record at all. It can indicate what concerns and conditions of trust this population articulates: strong concerns about data privacy and misuse, recognition of potential support for reminders, mental health and daily functioning, greater trust where tools were personalised, human-centred and co-developed, and residual worry about loss of critical thinking and overreliance. It cannot establish how common any of those views are, nor separate the views of people with schizophrenia spectrum disorder from those with bipolar disorder or major depression, because the abstract reports no participant count and no diagnostic breakdown. Indicative rather than moderate for two reasons stated in the abstract itself: it is a **secondary analysis** of three focus groups collected for another purpose, and the full text could not be reached to appraise the sampling, coding or reflexivity.

It establishes nothing empirical: a classification carries no prevalence, no effect and no mechanism, and the consensus process behind it is not an evidence synthesis. Strong for definitional use only; the tier would be meaningless applied to any other use.

unplaced.authors: Wunderink, L., Nieboer, R. M., Wiersma, D., Sytema, S. & Nienhuis, F. J.
unplaced.title: Recovery in remitted first-episode psychosis at 7 years of follow-up of an early dose reduction/discontinuation or maintenance treatment strategy: long-term follow-up of a 2-year randomized clinical trial.
unplaced.strength_why: A seven-year follow-up of a randomised trial in remitted first-episode psychosis with 80.5% of the original randomised sample located, reporting that the dose-reduction/discontinuation arm had twice the recovery rate of the maintenance arm (40.4% versus 17.6%, OR 3.49, P = .01), driven by functional rather than symptomatic remission. It is the only source found that disconfirms the straightforward 'stay on medication' reading of the relapse evidence, and it does so in exactly the vignette's population — a first episode, in remission. It CANNOT bear a recommendation: the randomisation governed only the first 18 months and treatment after the 2-year trial was 'at the discretion of the clinician', so the seven-year comparison is observational in all but name; it was an open (unblinded) trial; 111 of 257 eligible patients refused, which is a severe selection problem; n is 103 and the primary outcome was not the original trial's; and the authors say 'additional studies are necessary before these results are incorporated into general practice'. Moderate, and the reason is the 18-month randomisation window, not the finding.

unplaced.authors: Xia, J., Merinder, L. B. & Belgamwar, M. R.
unplaced.title: Psychoeducation for schizophrenia.
unplaced.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 44 RCTs and 5142 participants reporting that psychoeducation reduces non-compliance (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.67, NNT 11), relapse (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.81, NNT 9) and readmission (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89, NNT 5), with better social and global functioning and higher service satisfaction. It can establish that patient education is a treatment component with trial evidence behind it rather than a courtesy, which is what `e2-plan` needs. It CANNOT be taken at the size reported: the authors state plainly that 'the true size of effect is likely to be less than demonstrated in this review', risk of bias was rated moderate, the trials are mostly inpatient and median duration is only about 12 weeks, and the register search ends in February 2010. Moderate on the authors' own effect-size caveat and the inpatient setting, which is a poor match for a college student in the community.

unplaced.authors: Yang, Q., Wu, H., Du, X., Sun, Q. & Ren, Z.
unplaced.title: Emotional support or problem-solving? A randomized controlled trial of function-specific AI chatbots for digital stress in college students.
unplaced.strength_why: A genuine three-arm randomised controlled trial with a waitlist control in the vignette's population — university students, selected for elevated digital stress — which is a design the AI-and-mental-health corpus otherwise does not contain at all, and with Chinese participants, which the corpus badly needs. It can establish that a 14-day self-guided generative-AI chatbot can reduce specific dimensions of digital stress, and that function matters: the emotional-support bot reduced availability stress, approval anxiety, social comparison stress and fear of missing out, while the problem-solving bot was better at reducing online vigilance. It CANNOT bear weight on psychosis: there is no psychosis or psychosis-risk outcome anywhere in it, the sample is 99 across three arms so roughly 33 per cell, the follow-up is 14 days, and 'both interventions significantly alleviated anxiety symptoms, whereas effects on depressive symptoms were not significant' — a split result the essay should report rather than round up. Indicative: strong design, very small, very short, and wrong outcome for the claim it would be asked to support.

unplaced.authors: Yung, A. R., Yuen, H. P., McGorry, P. D., Phillips, L. J., Kelly, D., Dell'Olio, M., Francey, S. M., Cosgrave, E. M., Killackey, E., Stanford, C., Godfrey, K. & Buckby, J.
unplaced.title: Mapping the onset of psychosis: the Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States.
unplaced.strength_why: The paper that introduced the CAARMS, reporting what its own authors twice call a pilot and preliminary evaluation: concurrent, discriminant and predictive validity plus inter-rater reliability, tested in an ultra high risk group, a control group and 150 non-psychotic help-seekers followed for six months. It can establish that the instrument exists, what it is for (assessing psychopathology indicating imminent first-episode psychosis, and determining whether a person meets ultra high risk criteria), and that CAARMS-positive help-seekers transitioned at a higher rate than CAARMS-negative ones. It cannot establish how much higher with any useful precision: the relative risk of 12.44 carries a 95% confidence interval of 1.5 to 103.41, a range spanning nearly two orders of magnitude, and the follow-up was six months. Rated indicative rather than moderate on the authors' own description of it as a pilot, on that interval, and because the full text could not be reached, so the UHR and control group sizes, the transition counts and the reliability coefficients are all unverified.

unplaced.authors: Zhang, Y., Zhao, D., Hancock, J. T., Kraut, R. & Yang, D.
unplaced.title: Interaction with AI companions and psychological well-being
unplaced.strength_why: The only source found that separates companionship use of a chatbot from instrumental use in real users and attaches an outcome to the distinction, and it does so with behavioural evidence — 464687 messages from donated chat logs — rather than self-report alone, which is what the rest of this corpus runs on. It CAN establish that among 1131 Character.AI users the association between AI companionship and well-being is conditional: reporting companionship as the primary use was associated with lower well-being (beta -0.48, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.25), more so when interactions were intensive (-0.31, CI -0.56 to -0.06) and highly disclosive (-0.38, CI -0.63 to -0.14), and smaller offline social networks were associated with reporting companionship as the primary use (beta -0.03, CI -0.05 to -0.01). It CANNOT establish direction or drift: the design is cross-sectional, so a small social network preceding companionship use and companionship use shrinking a social network fit the data equally, and nothing in it tracks a person moving from instrumental to companion use over time. Nor can it bear weight on psychosis: there is no psychosis or psychosis-risk measure. Moderate: a large, well-reported study in a strong venue with behavioural triangulation and confidence intervals, limited by a self-selected sample of users of one product, a US-only frame, a cross-sectional design, and a record read from the abstract only because the paper is paywalled.

unplaced.authors: Zhu, Y., Krause, M., Huhn, M., Rothe, P., Schneider-Thoma, J., Chaimani, A., Li, C., Davis, J. M. & Leucht, S.
unplaced.title: Antipsychotic drugs for the acute treatment of patients with a first episode of schizophrenia: a systematic review with pairwise and network meta-analyses.
unplaced.strength_why: The dedicated first-episode evidence synthesis for acute antipsychotic treatment: 19 RCTs, 12 drugs, 2669 participants, with SMDs and ORs and 95% CIs, searching seven databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov without language restriction. It can establish that haloperidol is a suboptimal first choice in first-episode schizophrenia, that differences between second-generation drugs are small, and — the finding that matters most for a treatment plan — that 'the choice of treatment should be guided primarily by side-effects'. It CANNOT support a claim that any particular drug is best: the authors state the evidence was 'generally of low quality' and 'the numbers of patients for each drug were small', the significant effects against haloperidol are small (SMD -0.14 to -0.37) with intervals reaching -0.01, and tolerability findings are graded very low to low quality. Moderate rather than strong on the authors' own quality assessment of the underlying trials.

unplaced.authors: Zubin, J. & Spring, B.
unplaced.title: Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia
unplaced.strength_why: A theoretical paper, not an empirical study, and the originating statement of the stress-vulnerability model of schizophrenia: it is cited because it is the source of the concept, which is exactly the use foundational work is for. Its age is not a weakness here - a 1977 paper is the correct citation for a 1977 idea, and citing a 2020s textbook for it instead would be a weaker reference, not a stronger one. What it cannot do is carry any empirical weight: it predates neuroimaging, molecular genetics and every modern incidence study, so any claim about the size or mechanism of a risk factor must be cited to current evidence and never to this. Indicative per the tier definition for foundational theory papers; the rating is of evidential weight, not of importance.
